definition: Someone for whom hope has been abandoned.
A ship abandoned on the high seas.
Of or relating to or near the abdomen.
example: Abdominal muscles.
etymology: First attested in 1746. From New Latin abdōminālis, from Latin abdōmen. Equivalent to abdomin- + -al. Compare French abdominal.

definition: Breathing in which most of the respiratory effort is done by the abdominal muscles.
example: Abdominal breathing is practiced by singers.

definition: The delivery of a fetus by surgical incision through the abdominal wall and uterus (from the belief that Julius Caesar was born that way).
The muscles of the abdomen.
Ectopic pregnancy in the abdominal cavity.
A wall of the abdomen.
Dwell.
example: The old oak tree abides the wind endlessly.
etymology: Cognate with Scots abide (“to abide, remain”), Middle High German erbīten (“to await, expect”), Gothic 𐌿𐍃𐌱𐌴𐌹𐌳𐌰𐌽 (usbeidan, “to expect, await, have patience”). The sense of pay for is due to influence from aby.

definition: Act in accordance with someone's rules, commands, or wishes.
example: Abide by the rules.

definition: Not normal; not typical or usual or regular or conforming to a norm.
example: Abnormal powers of concentration.
etymology: From ab- + normal.

definition: The branch of psychology concerned with abnormal behavior.
Characteristic of or relating to people inhabiting a region from the beginning.
example: The aboriginal peoples of Australia.
etymology: See Aboriginal.

definition: Quickly and without warning.
example: The professor stopped her lecture abruptly when she noticed someone fall off their seat.
etymology: From abrupt + -ly.

definition: The occurrence of an abrupt, transient loss or impairment of consciousness (which is not subsequently remembered), sometimes with light twitching, fluttering eyelids, etc.; common in petit mal epilepsy.
Pure ethyl alcohol (containing no more than 1% water).
The number of observations in a given statistical category.
(elections) more than half of the votes.
The ability to identify the pitch of a tone.
A temperature scale that defines absolute zero as 0 degrees; water freezes at 273.16 degrees and boils at 373.16 degrees.
Temperature measured on the absolute scale.
Capable of arousing and holding the attention.
example: An absorbing pursuit.
etymology: From absorb + -ing.

definition: (chemistry) a process in which one substance permeates another; a fluid permeates or is dissolved by a liquid or solid.
example: The sponge showed remarkable absorption of water.
etymology: First attested in 1597. From Latin absorptiō (“a sucking in”), from absorbeō (“absorb”). Morphologically absorb + -tion.

definition: A dark band in the spectrum of white light that has been transmitted through a substance that exhibits absorption at selective wavelengths.
(physics) the property of a body that determines the fraction of the incident radiation or sound flux absorbed or absorbable by the body.
The spectrum of electromagnetic radiation that has passed through a medium that absorbed radiation of certain wavelengths.
A unit for measuring absorption.
Consider a concept without thinking of a specific example; consider abstractly or theoretically.
example: The young stranger had been abstracted and silent.
etymology: From Middle English abstract, borrowed from Latin abstractus, perfect passive participle of abstrahō (“draw away”), formed from abs- (“away”) + trahō (“to pull, draw”). The verbal sense is first attested in 1542.

definition: An abstract genre of art; artistic content depends on internal form rather than pictorial representation.
Thinking that is coherent and logical.
Present in great quantity.
example: An abundant supply of water.
etymology: First attested about 1380. From Middle English abundaunt, habundaunt, aboundant, from Anglo-Norman abundant, from Old French abondant, from Latin abundāns, present participle of abundō (“to overflow, to abound”).

definition: The academic world.
example: Academia continues to provide scientific education, despite attempts to turn it into a system of professional schooling.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin acadēmīa, from Ancient Greek Ἀκαδημία (Akadēmía), a grove of trees and gymnasium outside of Athens where Plato taught;

definition: The freedom of teachers and students to express their ideas in school without religious or political or institutional restrictions.
etymology: Calque of German akademische Freiheit. First attested in English in 1901.

definition: A gown worn by academics or judges.
A professional relation between instructors and those they instruct.
The time during which a school holds classes.
Move faster.
example: The car accelerated.
etymology: First attested in the 1520s.

definition: Speeded up, as of an academic course.
example: In an accelerated program in school.

definition: A unit for measuring acceleration.
Worthy of acceptance or satisfactory.
example: Acceptable levels of radiation.
etymology: From Middle English acceptable, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French acceptable, from Late Latin acceptābilis (“worthy of acceptance”). Morphologically accept + -able.

definition: The mental attitude that something is believable and should be accepted as true.
example: Acceptance of Newtonian mechanics was unquestioned for 200 years.
etymology: * First attested in 1528–1530. Probably partly from Middle French acceptance (from Old French accepter (“accept”)) and partly from accept + -ance.

definition: A statistical procedure for accepting or rejecting a batch of merchandise or documents; involves determining the maximum number of defects discovered in a sample before the entire batch is rejected.
Tolerating without protest.
example: Always more accepting of coaching suggestion than her teammates.

definition: The quality of being at hand when needed.
etymology: From accessible + -ity, after Late Latin accessibilitas, from Latin accessibilis.

definition: Capable of being reached.
example: A town accessible by rail.
etymology: First attested in 1400, from French, from Late Latin accessibilis, from accessus, perfect passive participle of accēdō (“approach”), equivalent to access + -ible.

definition: Clothing that is worn or carried, but not part of your main clothing.
etymology: From Medieval Latin accessōrius, from Latin accessor (“helper, subordinate”), from accessus. Compare access, from same root.

definition: Fruit containing much fleshy tissue besides that of the ripened ovary; as apple or strawberry.
Arises from two sets of roots (cranial and spinal) that unite to form the nerve.
The branch of medicine that deals with the surgical repair of injuries and wounds arising from accidents.
An accident that results in physical damage or hurt.
Without advance planning.
example: They met accidentally.
etymology: From accidental + -ly.

definition: (nautical) a portable ladder hung over the side of a vessel to give access to small boats alongside.
Having companions or an escort.
example: There were lone gentlemen and gentlemen accompanied by their wives.

definition: A vein accompanying another structure; a vein may accompany an artery in such a way that the arterial pulses aid venous return.
Highly skilled.
example: An accomplished pianist.
etymology: * First attested in the late 15th century, from accomplish + -ed.

definition: An irreversible accomplishment.
The action of accomplishing something.
example: The accomplishment of an enterprise, of a prophecy, etc.
etymology: * First attested in the early 15th century. * (completes, perfects, equips): First attested around 1600. * accomplish + -ment * Borrowed from French accomplissement, from accomplir

definition: Concurrence of opinion.
example: We are in accord with your proposal.
etymology: * (compliance): First attested around 1300. * (agreement): First attested in the early 14th century. * accord + -ance * From Middle English accordaunce, from Old French acordance (“agreeing, reconciliation, harmony”).

definition: Someone who maintains and audits business accounts.
etymology: From Middle English, from Middle French acuntant. Equivalent to account + -ant. First attested in the mid 15th century.

definition: A convincing explanation that reveals basic causes.
example: He was unable to give a clear accounting for his actions.
etymology: * First attested in the late 14th century. * account + -ing

definition: All the data (ledgers and journals and spreadsheets) that support a financial statement; can be hard copy or machine readable.
A written record of a commercial transaction.
A firm of accountants who provide accounting and auditing services for a fee.
A principle that governs current accounting practice and that is used as a reference to determine the appropriate treatment of complex transactions.
A bookkeeper's chronological list of related debits and credits of a business; forms part of a ledger of accounts.
The act of granting credit or recognition (especially with respect to an educational institution that maintains suitable standards).
example: A commission is responsible for the accreditation of medical schools.
etymology: First attested in 1806, from accredit + -ation.

definition: Given official approval to act.
example: An accredited college.
etymology: * accredit + -ed * From the French accréditer. * See credit.

definition: Periodically accumulated over time.
An increase by natural growth or addition.
A formal charge of wrongdoing brought against a person; the act of imputing blame or guilt.
example: Ungrounded accusations.
etymology: First attested in the late 14th century. Inherited from Middle English accusacion, borrowed from Old French acusacion (French: accusation), from Latin accūsātiō (“accusation, indictment”), from accūsō (“blame, accuse”).

definition: Bring an accusation against; level a charge against.
example: The neighbors accused the man of spousal abuse.
etymology: First attested around 1300. From Middle English acusen, from Old French acuser, from Latin accūsō (“to call to account, accuse”), from ad (“to”) + causa (“cause, lawsuit, reason”). Akin to cause.

definition: Containing or expressing accusation.
example: An accusative forefinger.

definition: Commonly used or practiced; usual.
example: His accustomed thoroughness.
etymology: From accustom + -ed.

definition: In the habit of or adapted to.
example: Accustomed to doing her own work.

definition: The action of accomplishing something.
example: Finishing the game does not give you a 100% score until you have unlocked all of the achievements.
etymology: From Middle French achevement (compare Modern French achèvement), from Old French achevement, from the verb achever, achiever (“to finish”); equivalent to achieve + -ment.

definition: Dye in which the chromophore is part of a negative ion.
Rain containing acids that form in the atmosphere when industrial gas emissions (especially sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides) combine with water.
Rain containing acids that form in the atmosphere when industrial gas emissions (especially sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides) combine with water.
etymology: Coined in 1872 by Scottish chemist Robert Angus Smith.

definition: A musical style that emerged in the 1960s; rock music inspired by or related to drug-induced experience.
A rigorous or crucial appraisal.
etymology: From acid + test;

definition: (chemistry) the amount of free acid present in fat as measured by the milligrams of potassium hydroxide needed to neutralize it.
example: As the glycerides in fat slowly decompose, the acid value increases.

definition: Not easily decolorized by acid solutions; pertains to micro-organisms (especially the tubercle bacillus that causes tuberculosis).
Thriving in a relatively acidic environment (especially of plants requiring a pH well below 7).
Having a sour acidic taste.
Wash with acid so as to achieve a bleached look.
example: Acid-wash blue jeans.

definition: Declare to be true or admit the existence or reality or truth of.
example: She acknowledged that she might have forgotten.
etymology: Recorded since 1553, a blend of Middle English aknowen (“to recognize, acknowledge”) and knowlechen (“to discover, reveal, acknowledge”).

definition: An inflammatory disease involving the sebaceous glands of the skin; characterized by papules or pustules or comedones.
example: He struggled with severe acne during his teenage years.
etymology: From New Latin acnē, probably a corruption of Ancient Greek ἀκμή (akmḗ, “point, top”).

definition: A composite sensory nerve supplying the hair cells of the vestibular organ and the hair cells of the cochlea.
A physical phenomenon associated with the production or transmission of sound.
The acoustic phenomenon that gives sound a penetrating quality.
Personal knowledge or information about someone or something.
example: I know of the man; but have no acquaintance with him.
etymology: From Middle English aqueyntaunce, from Anglo-Norman aquaintaunce, aqueintance, Old French acointance (“friendship, familiarity”), from Old French acointier (“to acquaint”). Compare French accointance.

definition: Having fair knowledge of.
example: They were acquainted.

definition: A preference that is only acquired after considerable experience.
example: Martinis are an acquired taste.

definition: The act of contracting or assuming or acquiring possession of something.
example: The acquisition of wealth.
etymology: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French acquisicion, from Latin acquisītiō, from acquīrō, acquīrere; equivalent to acquire + -ition.

definition: Contract governing the merger of two or more companies.
Extensive landed property (especially in the country) retained by the owner for their own use.
example: For quotations using this term, see Citations:acres.

definition: The operating part that transmits power to a mechanism.
example: The piano had a very stiff action.

definition: The efficiency with which electromagnetic radiation produces a photochemical reaction plotted as a function of the wavelength of the radiation.
Put in motion or move to act.
example: Activate the economy.
etymology: From active + -ate.

definition: A citizen who takes an active role in the community (as in crime prevention and neighborhood watch).
A policy of taking direct action to achieve a political or social goal.
etymology: From active + -ism.

definition: (law) immediate and direct physical control over property.
A sin committed of your own free will (as contrasted with original sin).
A mark placed above a vowel to indicate pronunciation.
etymology: From Latin accentus (“accent”) acūtus (“sharp”), a calque of Ancient Greek προσῳδία (prosōidía, “accent”) ὀξύς (oxús, “sharp”). Cognate to French accent aigu.

definition: A triangle whose interior angles are all acute.
An organized program of advertisements.
Without advance preparation.
example: He spoke ad lib.
etymology: Abbreviation of ad libitum, borrowed from New Latin ad libitum.

definition: In proportion to the estimated value of the goods taxed.
example: The goods were taxed ad valorem.

definition: With little or no preparation or forethought.
example: His ad-lib comments showed poor judgment.

definition: A musician who adapts a composition for particular voices or instruments or for another style of performance.
Having a capacity for adaptation.
example: The adaptive coloring of a chameleon.
etymology: From adapt + -ive.

definition: The development of many different forms from an originally homogeneous group of organisms as they fill different ecological niches.
Someone who is so ardently devoted to something that it resembles an addiction.
example: A golf addict.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin addictus, past participle of addīcō (“deliver; devote; surrender”), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + dīcō (“say; declare”)

definition: Causing or characterized by addiction.
example: Addictive drugs.
etymology: First attested 1914. Addiction in modern sense is first attested 1906, in reference to opium. There is an isolated instance from 1779, with reference to tobacco.

definition: In addition, by way of addition; furthermore.
example: He serves additionally as the CEO.
etymology: From additional + -ly.

definition: (of mail) marked with a destination.
example: I throw away all mail addressed to ‘resident’.

definition: In an adequate manner or to an adequate degree.
example: He was adequately prepared.
etymology: From adequate + -ly.

definition: Be compatible or in accordance with.
example: You must adhere to the rules.
etymology: From Middle English *adheren (suggested by Middle English adherande (“adhering, adherent”, present participle)), from Latin adhaerēre, adhaesum: ad (“to”) + haerēre (“to stick”). Compare French adhérer.

definition: Capable of being changed so as to match or fit.
example: Adjustable seat belts.
etymology: From adjust + -able.

definition: An accounting entry made at the end of an accounting period to allocate items between accounting periods.
Work in an administrative capacity; supervise or be in charge of.
example: Administer a program.
etymology: From Middle English administren, from Old French aminister, from Latin administrare (“to manage, execute”), from ad (“to”) + ministrare (“to attend, serve”), from minister (“servant”); see minister.

definition: A hearing that takes place outside the judicial process before hearing examiners who have been granted judicial authority specifically for the purpose of conducting such hearings.
A unit with administrative responsibilities.
A feeling of delighted approval and liking.
example: Admiration of a war hero.
etymology: From Middle English admiracion, borrowed from Middle French admiration, or directly from Latin admīrātiō, from prefix ad- (“to, towards”) + mīrō (“to look at”) + -ātiō.

definition: Regarded with admiration.
The act of admitting someone to enter.
example: The surgery was performed on his second admission to the clinic.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin admissio, admissionis; compare French admission. See admit.

definition: The fee charged for admission.
As acknowledged.
example: Admittedly, vandalism is a bit of a problem.
etymology: From admitted + -ly.

definition: The clay from which adobe bricks are made.
example: Many people in Texas and New Mexico live in adobe houses.
etymology: From Spanish adobe, from Arabic اَلطُّوب (aṭ-ṭūb), from Sahidic Coptic ⲧⲱⲃⲉ (tōbe, “brick”), from Demotic Egyptian ⁠⁠ (tb, “brick”), from Egyptian Db-b-t:O39 (ḏbt, “brick, block, ingot”).

definition: A house built of sod or adobe laid in horizontal courses.
Relating to or peculiar to or suggestive of an adolescent.
example: Adolescent problems.

definition: Love intensely.
example: He just adored his wife.
etymology: From Middle English *adoren, aouren, from Old French adorer, aorer, from Latin adōrō (“to pray to”), from ad (“to”) + ōrō (“to speak”).

definition: A catecholamine secreted by the adrenal medulla in response to stress (trade name Adrenalin); stimulates autonomic nerve action.
The period of time in your life after your physical growth has stopped and you are fully developed.
example: Meronyms: young adulthood; emerging adulthood (sometimes construed as coordinate).
etymology: From adult + -hood.

definition: Arrival that has been awaited (especially of something momentous).
example: The advent of the computer.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin adventus (“arrival, approach”).

definition: Call attention to.
example: Please don't advertise the fact that he has AIDS.

definition: Called to public attention.
example: These advertised products.

definition: An agency that designs advertisement to call public attention to its clients.
A board appointed to advise the chief administrator.
A consulting service in which a CPA develops findings and conclusions and recommendations that are presented to the client for consideration and decision making.
Mechanically extendible ladder; used on a fire truck.
The atmosphere and outer space considered as a whole.
example: He works mainly in aerospace. Most of their contracts are in aerospace. A few are in medical devices.
etymology: From aero- + space.

definition: An engineer of aircraft and space vehicles.
The study and treatment of disorders associated with flight (especially with space flight).
(art) the branch of philosophy dealing with beauty and taste (emphasizing the evaluative criteria that are applied to art).
example: Traditional aesthetics assumed the existence of universal and timeless criteria of artistic value.
etymology: From aesthetic + -s.

definition: A social or business relationship.
example: A valuable financial affiliation.
etymology: From French affiliation, from Latin affiliatiō, noun of action from verb affiliō, from af- (form of ad- (“to”) before an f) + filiō (from filius (“son”)).

definition: (immunology) the attraction between an antigen and an antibody.
etymology: From Middle English affinite, from Old French affinité. Ostensibly equivalent to affine + -ity. See also af-.

definition: Affirming or giving assent.
example: An affirmative decision.
etymology: From Middle English affirmative, affirmatyve, from Old French affirmatif, from Latin affirmativus, from affirmare (“to assert”).

definition: A policy designed to redress past discrimination against women and minority groups through measures to improve their economic and educational opportunities.
example: Affirmative action has been extremely controversial and was challenged in 1978 in the Bakke decision.

definition: That you have the financial means for.
example: An affordable vacation in the local area.
etymology: From afford + -able.

definition: Being the one previously mentioned or spoken of.
example: Works of all the aforementioned authors.
etymology: From afore- + mentioned.

definition: One of the items to be considered.
Having or showing determination and energetic pursuit of your ends.
example: An aggressive businessman.
etymology: From aggress + -ive. Compare with French agressif.

definition: In an aggressive manner.
etymology: From aggressive + -ly.

definition: Intense feelings of suffering; acute mental or physical pain.
example: An agony of doubt.
etymology: 14th century, via Old French and Latin from Ancient Greek ἀγωνία (agōnía, “emulation, competition, struggle”), from ἀγών (agṓn, “contest”). Specifically of the struggle that precedes death (mortal agony) from the 1540s.

definition: A newspaper column devoted to personal problems.
A male newspaper columnist who answers questions and offers advice on personal problems to people who write in.
etymology: By analogy with earlier agony aunt, from still earlier agony column.

definition: An advisor employed by the government to assist people in rural areas with methods of farming and home economics.
A large-scale farming enterprise.
An officer who acts as military assistant to a more senior officer.
etymology: Borrowed from French aide ("aid; assistant", as in aide-de-camp (“field assistant”)). More at aid.

definition: Having help; often used as a combining form.
The time period during which military and civilian agencies are prepared for an enemy air attack.
An air-filled sac near the spinal column in many fishes that helps maintain buoyancy.
A bubble of air.
The trapped air that supports a hovercraft a short distance above the water or ground.
A duct that provides ventilation (as in mines).
A filter that removes dust from the air that passes through it.
A hammer driven by compressed air.
A pneumatic horn.
A hose that carries air under pressure.
etymology: From air + hose.

definition: An inflatable life jacket.
A mattress that can be stored flat and inflated for use.
etymology: From air + mattress.

definition: A duct that provides ventilation (as in mines).
Pollution of the atmosphere.
example: Air pollution reduced the visibility.

definition: A pump that moves air in or out of something.
An attack by armed planes on a surface target.
A tiny sac for holding air in the lungs; formed by the terminal dilation of tiny air passageways.
A truncated cloth cone mounted on a mast; used (e.g., at airports) to show the direction of the wind.
A terminal that serves air travelers or air freight.
Someone who travels by airplane.
Deriving oxygen from the air.
example: He studied respiration in marine air-breathing vertebrates.

definition: Cooled by air conditioning.
example: Our servers are kept in an air-conditioned room.

definition: Cooled by a flow of air.
example: An air-cooled engine.

definition: Moved or conveyed by or through air.
example: Airborne pollen can aggravate allergies.
etymology: Attested since the 1640s; air + -borne

definition: A patrol provided by aircraft.
A transmission mechanism in the which the infectious agent is spread as an aerosol and usually enters a person through the respiratory tract.
A large warship that carries planes and has a long flat deck for takeoffs and landings.
Landing an aircraft.
The opening of a subject to widespread discussion and debate.
example: Airing of grievances.
etymology: From air (“substance constituting Earth’s atmosphere”, noun) and air (“to bring (something) into contact with the air; to let fresh air into (a place); to make public (an opinion, etc.);

definition: The craft of building and repairing airplanes.
A terminal that serves air travelers or air freight.
Affected manners intended to impress others.
example: Don't put on airs with me.

definition: A long narrow passage (as in a cave or woods).
example: Do you want to seat window or aisle?
etymology: From Middle English ele, from Anglo-Norman ele (“wing”) (Modern French aile), from Latin āla (whence English ala). Further from Latin axis (whence English axis, atelier).

definition: Similar in quality or character.
example: A feeling akin to terror.
etymology: From a corruption of of kin, from Middle English of kyn (“related, of kin”), equivalent to a- + kin (1550s). Compare Old English cyn, cynn (“akin, proper, suitable”, adj.).

definition: A flat wing-shaped process or winglike part of an organism.
example: The alae of the nose.
etymology: Originated 1730–40, borrowed from Latin āla (“wing”). Doublet of aisle.

definition: The sound of an alarm (usually a bell).
A device that signals the occurrence of some undesirable event.
Frightening because of an awareness of danger.
By bad luck.
example: Alas, I cannot stay.
etymology: From Middle English alas, from Old French a las (French hélas), from a (“ah”) + las, from Latin lassus (“weary”). Compare Dutch helaas, North Frisian ielas, West Frisian eilaas.

definition: Excessive use of alcohol and alcoholic drinks.
The chemical group -OH.
Addicted to alcohol.
example: Alcoholic expatriates in Paris.

definition: Dementia observed during the last stages of severe chronic alcoholism; involves loss of memory for recent events although long term memory is intact.
A general name for beer made with a top fermenting yeast; in some of the United States an ale is (by law) a brew of more than 4% alcohol by volume.
Primitive chlorophyll-containing mainly aquatic eukaryotic organisms lacking true stems and roots and leaves.
The mathematics of generalized arithmetical operations.
A person who comes from a foreign country; someone who does not owe allegiance to your country.
etymology: From Middle English alien, a borrowing from Old French alien, aliene, from Latin aliēnus (“belonging to someone else”, later “exotic, foreign”), from Latin alius (“other”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élyos.

definition: Place in a line or arrange so as to be parallel or straight.
example: Align the car with the curb.

definition: An organization of people (or countries) involved in a pact or treaty.
example: The alignment problem.
etymology: From French alignement, by surface analysis, align + -ment.

definition: Broad in scope or content.
example: An all-embracing definition.
etymology: From all + embracing.

definition: Never having lost.
(law) a formal accusation against somebody (often in a court of law).
example: An allegation of malpractice.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French allégation, from Latin allegatio, from allegare. By surface analysis, allege + -ation, see allege.

definition: The act of binding yourself (intellectually or emotionally) to a course of action.
etymology: From Middle English alegiaunce, from Anglo-Norman alegaunce (“loyalty of a liege-servant to one's lord”), variant of Old French ligeance, from lige (“vassal, liegeman”). More at liege.

definition: Characterized by or caused by allergy.
example: An allergic reaction.
etymology: From allergy + -ic.

definition: Hypersensitivity reaction to a particular allergen; symptoms can vary greatly in intensity.
A diet designed to avoid the foods that you are allergic to.
Provide physical relief, as from pain.
example: Alleviate his pain.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin alleviatus, past participle of alleviāre (“to lighten; to alleviate”). By surface analysis, al- + Latin lev- + -i- + -ate.

definition: A share set aside for a specific purpose.
example: The allocation of new permits is on a first-come, first-served basis.
etymology: From Middle French allocacion, from Medieval Latin allocātiō. By surface analysis, allocate + -ion.

definition: A group of sectors on a magnetic disk that can be reserved for the use of a particular file.
A mixture containing two or more metallic elements or metallic and nonmetallic elements usually fused together or dissolving into each other when molten.
example: Brass is an alloy of zinc and copper.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French alloy, aloy, from Old French aloi, from aloiier, from Latin alligō.

definition: Cast iron containing alloying elements (usually nickel or chromium or copper or molybdenum) to increase the strength or facilitate heat treatment.
Steel who characteristics are determined by the addition of other elements in addition to carbon.
Unite formally; of interest groups or countries.
Having unlimited power.
example: God almighty.
etymology: From Middle English almyghty, almighty, from Old English ælmihtiġ (“all-powerful”), from Proto-Germanic *alamahtīgaz, equivalent to al- + might + -y.

definition: Small bushy deciduous tree native to Asia and North Africa having pretty pink blossoms and highly prized edible nuts enclosed in a hard green hull; cultivated in southern Australia and California.
etymology: Pronunciations with /l/ are likely originally spelling pronunciations;

definition: Pale yellow fatty oil expressed from sweet or bitter almonds.
Any of several small bushy trees having pink or white blossoms and usually bearing nuts.
Using the voice; not silently.
example: Please read the passage aloud.
etymology: From Middle English aloud, a loude (“aloud”), equivalent to a- + loud or a- + loude (“sound”).

definition: Radioactive decay of an atomic nucleus that is accompanied by the emission of an alpha particle.
A magnetic allotrope of iron; stable below 906 degrees centigrade.
A positively charged particle that is the nucleus of the helium atom; emitted from natural or radioactive isotopes.
The radiation of alpha particles during radioactive decay.
A first release of a software product that is usually tested only by the developers.
(computer science) a first test of an experimental product (such as computer software) carried out by the developer.
The normal brainwave in the electroencephalogram of a person who is awake but relaxed; occurs with a frequency of 8-12 hertz.
A character set that includes letters and is used to write a language.
example: The Greek alphabet has only twenty-four letters.
etymology: Doublet of alfabeto. Dipslaced native Old English stæfrǣw (literally "staff-row").

definition: A confusing assortment.
example: Roosevelt created an alphabet soup of federal agencies.

definition: Relating to or characteristic of alps.
example: Alpine sports.
etymology: From Latin Alpīnus, from Alpēs (“the Alps”). Cognates include French alpin.

definition: Tall timber tree with hard heavy pinkish or light brown wood.
Low tufted plant having hairy stems each topped by a flower head with short narrow yellow rays; northwestern United States.
A boy serving as an acolyte.
A girl serving as an acolyte.
Used in a communion service.
A very close and trusted friend who seems almost a part of yourself.
example: Clark Kent's coworkers finally discovered his alter ego, Superman.
etymology: From Latin alter ego (literally “other me”).

definition: The sterilization of an animal.
Go back and forth; swing back and forth between two states or conditions.
example: The flood and ebb tides alternate with each other.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin alternātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin alternō (“to take turns”) (see -ate (1,2 and 3)), from alternus (“one after another, by turns”), from alter (“other”) + -nus. Doublet of altern;

definition: (of a current) reversing direction.
example: Alternating current.

definition: A pleading that alleges facts so separate that it is difficult to determine which facts the person intends to rely on.
Effects (as nosebleed or nausea) of oxygen deficiency in the blood and tissues at high altitudes.
A silvery ductile metallic element found primarily in bauxite.
etymology: * For information on the origins of the two spellings, see the Wikipedia article.

definition: An alloy of copper and aluminum with high tensile strength and resistance to corrosion.
An alloy of copper and aluminum with high tensile strength and resistance to corrosion.
Foil made of aluminum.
Any of various forms of aluminum oxide occurring naturally as corundum.
In an amazing manner; to everyone's surprise.
example: Amazingly, he finished medical school in three years.
etymology: From amazing + -ly.

definition: A diplomat of the highest rank; accredited as representative from one country to another.

Plant having basal grasslike leaves and a narrow open cluster of starlike yellowish-orange flowers atop a leafless stalk; southwestern United States; only species of Anthericum growing in North America.
Completely enveloping.
example: The ambient air.
etymology: From Latin ambiēns (“going around”), from ambiō (“go around”).

definition: Open to two or more interpretations; or of uncertain nature or significance; or (often) intended to mislead.
example: The polling had a complex and equivocal (or ambiguous) message for potential female candidates.
etymology: From Latin ambiguus (“moving from side to side, of doubtful nature”), from ambigere (“to go about, wander, doubt”), from ambi- (“around, about, on both sides”) + agere (“to drive, move”).

definition: Wait in hiding to attack.
Congenital absence of an arm or leg.
etymology: From a- + Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos, “limb”) + -ia.

definition: Make amendments to.
example: Amend the document.
etymology: From Middle English amenden, from Old French amender, from Latin ēmendō (“free from faults”), from ex (“from, out of”) + mendum (“fault”). Compare aphetic mend. Doublet of emend.

definition: Of legislation.
example: We voted on the amended bill, and it passed.

definition: A tax return that corrects the information in an earlier return.
Things that make you comfortable and at ease.
example: The prime ministers engaged in diplomatic amenities before signing the treaty.

definition: Pertaining to or containing any of a group of organic compounds of nitrogen derived from ammonia.
etymology: From the prefix amino-, from amine, from ammonia + -ine.

definition: Organic compounds containing an amino group and a carboxylic acid group.
example: Proteins are composed of various proportions of about 20 common amino acids.
etymology: See amine and acid. Likely a calque of German Aminosäure, which is attested earlier.

definition: The radical -NH2.
A plastic (synthetic resin) made from amino compounds; used as an adhesive and as a coating for paper and textiles.
A period during which offenders are exempt from punishment.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French amnestie (Modern French amnistie), a borrowing from Latin amnestia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀμνηστία (amnēstía).

definition: More than enough in size or scope or capacity.
example: Had ample food for the party.
etymology: From late Middle English ample, from Middle French ample, from Latin amplus (“large”).

definition: Pleasantly occupied.
example: We are not amused.
etymology: From amuse + -ed.

definition: A feeling of delight at being entertained.
example: To my great amusement, the dog kept on chasing its tail and yelped when it bit it.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French amusement, from amuser + -ment. Morphologically amuse + -ment.

definition: A commercially operated park with stalls and shows for amusement.
Providing enjoyment; pleasantly entertaining.
example: An amusing speaker.
etymology: By surface analysis, amuse + -ing.

definition: Of a circuit or device having an output that is proportional to the input.
example: Analogue device.
etymology: First attested in the early 19th century; from French analogue, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλογος (análogos, “proportionate”), from ἀνά (aná, “up to”) + λόγος (lógos, “ratio”).

definition: A clock that displays the time of day by the position of hands on a dial.
etymology: This is a retronym coined when digital clocks became common.

definition: A computer that represents information by variable quantities (e.g., positions or voltages).
A watch that represents time by the position of hands on a dial.
An inference that if things agree in some respects they probably agree in others.
etymology: From Latin analogia, from Ancient Greek ἀναλογίᾱ (analogíā), from ἀνα- (ana-) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, reckoning”).

definition: Using or skilled in using analysis (i.e., separating a whole — intellectual or substantial — into its elemental parts or basic principles).
example: An analytic experiment.
etymology: Compare with French analytique. See analysis.

definition: A beam balance of great precision used in quantitative chemical analysis.
The use of algebra to study geometric properties; operates on symbols defined in a coordinate system.
An auditing procedure based on ratios among accounts and tries to identify significant changes.
The hereditary derivation of an individual.
example: I can trace my ancestry back to the 18th century.
etymology: From Middle English auncestrie, from Old French ancesserie. See ancestor.

definition: The chain or rope that attaches an anchor to a vessel.
A light sponge cake made without egg yolks.
A drug used as an anesthetic by veterinarians; illicitly taken (originally in the form of powder or ‘dust’) for its effects as a hallucinogen.
etymology: First attested in c. 1969 in Rolling Stone magazine.

definition: Either of two punctuation marks (‘<’ or ‘>’) used in computer programming and sometimes used to enclose textual material.
An L-shaped metal bracket.
Park at an angle.
Measured by an angle or by the rate of change of an angle.
example: Angular momentum.
etymology: From Middle English angular, anguler, from Latin angulāris, from angulus (“angle, corner”). See angle.

definition: Relation by which any position with respect to any other position is established.
Black substance containing char in the form of carbonized bone; used as a black pigment.
Fiber derived from animals.
A protein gelatin obtained by boiling e.g. skins and hoofs of cattle and horses.
The branch of psychology concerned with the behavior of animals.
A specialist in the branch of biology dealing with animals.
The tissue in the bodies of animals.
An animal pathogen that is a virus.
The worship of animals.
A film made by photographing a series of cartoon drawings to give the illusion of movement when projected in rapid sequence.
The condition of living or the state of being alive.
A boot that reaches to or just above the ankle.
A brace worn to strengthen the ankle.
An ornament worn around the ankle.
Take (territory) as if by conquest.
example: Hitler annexed Lithuania.
etymology: Borrowed from French annexe, from Latin annexus. More at Etymology 2. See also an-.

definition: A formal public statement.
example: The government made an announcement about changes in the drug war.
etymology: From Middle French annoncement. By surface analysis, announce + -ment.

definition: Someone who proclaims a message publicly.
Having no known name or identity or known source.
example: Anonymous authors.
etymology: Borrowed into English around 1600 from Late Latin anonymus, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓νώνῠμος (ănṓnŭmos, “without name”), from ᾰ̓ν- (ăn-, “un-”) with ὄνῠμᾰ (ónŭmă), Aeolic and Doric dialectal form of ὄνομᾰ (ónomă, “name”).

definition: Any of various dull-colored South American birds that feeding on ants some following army ant swarms.
Excretes a honeylike substance eaten by ants.
etymology: By analogy to the milking of a cow.

definition: The larva of any of several insects.
An electrical device that sends or receives radio or television signals.
Of or near the head end or toward the front plane of a body.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin anterior (“that is before, foremost”).

definition: The social science that studies the origins and social relationships of human beings.
example: According to anthropology, there are six basic patterns of kinship terminology or kin naming systems.
etymology: From New Latin anthropologia, from Ancient Greek ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “human, mankind”) + -λογία (-logía). By surface analysis, anthropo- + -logy.

definition: Opposition to democracy, typically, though not always, associated with anti-egalitarianism.
example: The anti-democracy of right-wing extremism includes an aversion to the democratic rules of the game.

definition: Opposed to the establishment.
example: The hippies were noted for their anti-establishment ways, firmly opposed to the order their parents so revered.
etymology: From anti- + establishment.

definition: A medicine intended to reduce inflammation.
etymology: From anti- + inflammatory.

definition: Smug and ignorant and indifferent or hostile to artistic and cultural values.
etymology: From anti- + intellectual.

definition: Relating to or characterized by anti-Semitism; hating Jews.
Of or relating to antibiotic drugs.
etymology: Borrowed from French antibiotique; by surface analysis, anti- + -biotic.

definition: Regard something as probable or likely.
example: The advocate plans to anticipate a part of her argument.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin anticipātus, perfect passive participle of anticipō (“to anticipate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ante- (“before”), + capiō (“to take”, cip- when prefixed) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

definition: An expectation.
example: Often the anticipation of a shot is worse than the pain of the stick.
etymology: From Middle English anticipacioun, from Middle French anticipation and its etymon Latin anticipātiō, anticipātiōnem. By surface analysis, anticipate + -ion.

definition: A sudden acute episode of intense anxiety and feelings of panic.

An anxiety disorder characterized by chronic free-floating anxiety and such symptoms as tension or sweating or trembling or lightheadedness or irritability etc. that has lasted for more than six months.
A Parisian gangster.
A violent fast dance in French vaudeville (an apache is a member of the French underworld).
A social policy or racial segregation involving political and economic and legal discrimination against people who are not Whites; the former official policy in South Africa.
example: The 1973 Apartheid Convention conferred universal jurisdiction to the state signatories to prosecute those who commit apartheid.
etymology: Borrowed from Afrikaans apartheid (literally “separateness, apartness”) (1929 in a South African socio-political context), from Afrikaans apart (“separate”) + suffix -heid, cognate of English -hood.

definition: The highest point (of something).
example: The apex of the building.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin apex (“point, tip, summit”).

definition: A cosmic cataclysm in which God destroys the ruling powers of evil.
example: The early development of Perl 6 was punctuated by a series of apocalypses by Larry Wall.
etymology: The verb is from the noun and, in sense 1, a semantic loan from the etymonic Ancient Greek verb ἀποκαλύπτω (apokalúptō, “to reveal”).

definition: Defend, explain, clear away, or make excuses for by reasoning.
etymology: From apology + -ise.

definition: Acknowledge faults or shortcomings or failing.
example: I apologized for being late.

definition: Equipment designed to serve a specific function.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin apparātus. Doublet of apparat.

definition: Clothing in general.
example: She was refined in her choice of apparel.
etymology: From Old French apareillier. Doublet of parrel.

definition: A chain of clothing stores.
Makers and sellers of fashionable clothing.
An optical illusion of motion produced by viewing a rapid succession of still pictures of a moving object.
example: The cinema relies on apparent motion.

definition: An optical illusion of motion produced by viewing a rapid succession of still pictures of a moving object.
example: The cinema relies on apparent motion.

definition: A board of officials that are not judicial but are appointed to hear appeals.
A court whose jurisdiction is to review decisions of lower courts or agencies.
Formal attendance (in court or at a hearing) of a party in an action.
Supplementary material that is collected and appended at the back of a book.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin appendix.

definition: Thick dark spicy puree of apples.
Jelly made from apple juice.
The juice of apples.
A grove of apple trees.
Rust fungus causing rust spots on apples and pears etc.
Puree of stewed apples usually sweetened and spiced.
Turnover with an apple filling.
Strong alcoholic beverage with apple flavour.
Having the general shape of an apple.
example: Apple-shaped obesity.

definition: Having the approximate size of an apple.
Capable of being applied; having relevance.
example: Gave applicable examples to support her argument.
etymology: From Old French applicable, from Medieval Latin applicabilis.

definition: A person who requests or seeks something such as assistance or employment or admission.
A program that gives a computer instructions that provide the user with tools to accomplish a task.
example: He has tried several different word processing applications.

definition: The branches of mathematics that are involved in the study of the physical or biological or sociological world.
Any of several branches of psychology that seek to apply psychological principles to practical problems of education or industry or marketing etc.
Create and charge with a task or function.
Fully understood or grasped.
example: Dangers not yet appreciated.

definition: Understanding of the nature or meaning or quality or magnitude of something.
example: We give to you this trophy as a token of our appreciation of all your years of service.
etymology: From French appréciation. By surface analysis, appreciate + -ion.

definition: Works for an expert to learn a trade.
etymology: From Middle English apprentice, apprentesse, apprentyse, apprentis, from Old French aprentis, plural of aprentif, from Old French aprendre (verb), Late Latin apprendō, from Classical Latin apprehendō.

definition: A trench that provides protected passage between the rear and front lines of a defensive position.
The event of one object coming closer to another.
etymology: By surface analysis, approach + -ing.

definition: In accordance with what is appropriate or suitable for the circumstances.
example: He was appropriately dressed.
etymology: From appropriate + -ly.

definition: Not quite exact or correct.
example: The approximate time was 10 o'clock.
etymology: From Middle English approximat(e) (“close, near (to); similar;

definition: Near to the scope or range of something.
(usually followed by ‘to’) naturally disposed toward.
example: He is apt to ignore matters he considers unimportant.
etymology: From Old French apte, from Latin aptus (“suitable, fitting”).

definition: A tank or pool or bowl filled with water for keeping live fish and underwater animals.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin aquārium, neuter of aquārius (“of or pertaining to water”), from aqua + -arium. Doublet of ewer; see also Aquarius.

definition: Relating to or consisting of or being in water.
example: An aquatic environment.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French aquatique (“living in water”), from Latin aquaticus (“relating to water”), from aqua (“water”).

definition: Wading and swimming and diving birds of either fresh or salt water.
A plant that grows partly or wholly in water whether rooted in the mud, as a lotus, or floating without anchorage, as the water hyacinth.
(law) the hearing and determination of a dispute by an impartial referee agreed to by both parties (often used to settle disputes between labor and management).
etymology: From Middle English arbitracion, borrowed from Old French arbitration, from Latin arbitratio, from arbitrari (“to arbitrate, judge”); see arbitrate.

definition: A clause in a contract providing for arbitration of disputes arising under the contract.
A lamp that produces light when electric current flows across the gap between two electrodes.
etymology: From arc + light.

definition: A covered passageway with shops and stalls on either side.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French arcade, from Italian arcata (“the arch of a bridge”), from Latin arcus (“an arc”). Not etymologically related to Arcadia.

definition: An action game characterised by short levels, simple and intuitive control schemes, and rapidly increasing difficulty.
Related to or dealing with or devoted to archaeology.
example: An archaeological dig.
etymology: From archaeology + -ical. By surface analysis, archaeo- + -logical.

definition: The branch of anthropology that studies prehistoric people and their cultures.
example: The building's developers have asked for some archaeology to be undertaken.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀρχαιολογία (arkhaiología, “antiquarian lore, ancient legends, history”), from ἀρχαῖος (arkhaîos, “primal, old, ancient”) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, oration, study”).

definition: An erect greyish branching lichen of Arctic and even some north temperate regions constituting the chief food for reindeer and caribou and sometimes being eaten by humans.
Low creeping shrub of Arctic Europe and America.
Any of various small silver-scaled salmon-like marine fishes.
etymology: From Middle English argentyne, borrowed from Old French argentin (“silvery”), from Latin argentum (“silver”), equivalent to argent + -ine.

definition: A boat built by Noah to save his family and animals from the flood.
Marine bivalve mollusk having a heavy toothed shell with a deep boat-like inner surface.
A bone in the arm.
An engagement fought between two military forces.
Protected by armor (used of persons or things military).
etymology: From armor + -ed.

definition: An armor-plated truck with strong doors and locks used to transport money or valuables.
example: The paintings were delivered to the museum in an air-conditioned armored car.

definition: Insect having a firm covering of wax especially in the female.
A vehicle that is protected by armor plate.
A military unit consisting of armored fighting vehicles.
Specially hardened steel plate used to protect fortifications or vehicles from enemy fire.
Someone who manufactures arms and munitions.
An army unit usually consisting of two or more divisions and their support.
A member of the military who is trained in engineering and construction work.
Noctuid moth larvae that travel in multitudes destroying especially grass and grain.
The thing arranged or agreed to.
example: They made arrangements to meet in Chicago.
etymology: From French arrangement. Morphologically arrange + -ment.

definition: The act of arranging and adapting a piece of music.
Commanding attention.
example: An arresting drawing of people turning into animals.

definition: Gate where passengers disembark.
Reach a destination, either real or abstract.
Overbearing pride evidenced by a superior manner toward inferiors.
etymology: From Middle English arrogaunce, from Middle French arrogance, from Latin arrogantia.

definition: Having or showing feelings of unwarranted importance out of overbearing pride.
example: An arrogant official.
etymology: From Middle English arrogaunt, from Old French arrogant, from Latin arrogāns, present active participle of arrogō.

definition: A dealer in works of art requiring esthetic evaluation.
An exhibition of art objects (paintings or statues).
A blood vessel that carries blood from the heart to the body.
etymology: Late Middle English arterie, borrowing from Old French artaire and Latin artēria (“a windpipe; an artery”), from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ρτηρῐ́ᾱ (ărtērĭ́ā, “windpipe; artery”).

definition: Inflammation of a joint or joints.
etymology: From Latin arthrītis, from Ancient Greek ἀρθρῖτις (arthrîtis, “joint-disease, gout”), from ἄρθρον (árthron, “a joint”). By surface analysis, arthr- + -itis.

definition: Provide with a joint.
example: I wish he’d articulate his words more clearly.
etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1531, the verb in 1551; borrowed from Latin articulātus (“distinct, articulated, jointed”), perfect passive participle of articulō, see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3).

definition: Contrived by art rather than nature.
example: Artificial flowers.

definition: A liquid that can carry large amounts of oxygen and can serve as a temporary substitute for blood.
A pump that replaces the natural heart.
A metal or plastic part that is surgically implanted to replace a natural joint (possibly elbow or wrist but usually hip or knee).
Lake used to store water for community use; a lake (natural or artificial) used to store water and used as a source of water.
A language that is deliberately created for a specific purpose.
A synthetic covering with two layers used experimentally to treat burn victims.
A constructed language designed for aesthetic pleasure.
A group of artists who agree on general principles.
The creation of beautiful or significant things.
The style of a particular artist or school or movement.
A fibrous amphibole; used for making fireproof articles; inhaling fibers can cause asbestosis or lung cancer.
example: All types of asbestos are potentially carcinogenic when inhaled.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin asbestos, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄσβεστος (ásbestos), from ἀ- (a-) + σβεστός (sbestós). Compare Middle English asbestus and Old French abestos.

definition: Towards the shore from the water.
example: We invited them ashore.
etymology: From a- + shore; see also onshore.

definition: Desiring or striving for recognition or advancement.
example: Aspiring pop stars lined up for hours just to audition.

definition: A true bug: long-legged predacious bug living mostly on other insects; a few suck blood of mammals.
etymology: From assassin + bug.

definition: Any of the automatic rifles or semiautomatic rifles with large magazines designed for military use.
Create by putting components or members together.
example: He assembled the model ship.

definition: State categorically.
example: He would often assert that there was life on other planets.
etymology: From Latin assertus, perfect passive participle of asserō (“declare someone free or a slave by laying hands upon him; hence free from, protect, defend;

definition: Confidently declared to be so.
example: The asserted value of the painting.

definition: A declaration that is made emphatically (as if no supporting evidence were necessary).
example: You're a man of strong assertions!
etymology: From Middle English assercioun, from Latin assertiō. By surface analysis, assert + -ion.

definition: Give an assignment to (a person) to a post, or assign a task to (a person).
example: To assign a day for trial.
etymology: From Middle English assignen, from Old French assigner, asigner, from Latin assignō, from ad- + signō (“mark, sign”).

definition: A duty that you are assigned to perform (especially in the armed forces).
example: Hazardous assignment.
etymology: From Middle English assignement, from Old French assignement. By surface analysis, assign + -ment.

definition: A member of a work gang who supervises the other workers.
A person who joins with others in some activity or endeavor.
example: He had to consult his associate before continuing.
etymology: From the substantivization of the above adjective, see -ate (noun-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

definition: A degree granted by a two-year college on successful completion of the undergraduates course of studies.
A teacher lower in rank than a full professor but higher than an assistant professor.
Cortical areas that are neither motor or sensory but are thought to be involved in higher processing of information.
A name that has been assumed.
Respiratory disorder characterized by wheezing; usually of allergic origin.
Surprising greatly.
example: The dog was capable of astonishing tricks.

definition: The branch of physics that studies celestial bodies and the universe as a whole.
etymology: From Middle English astronomie, astronemy, from Old French astronomie, equivalent to astro- + -nomy. Displaced native Old English tungolcræft.

definition: A satellite equipped with a telescope to observe infrared radiation.
A linear unit used for astronomical distances.
In disagreement.
example: The figures are at odds with our findings.
etymology: From at + odds (“(obsolete) dissimilarity; inequality”).

definition: In question or at issue.
example: There is more at stake than your modesty.

definition: Related to or characterized by or given to atheism.
example: Atheist leanings.
etymology: From Middle French athéiste (athée + -iste), from Latin atheos, from Ancient Greek ἄθεος (átheos, “godless, without god”), from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + θεός (theós, “god”).

definition: A game involving athletic activity.
A physical phenomenon associated with the atmosphere.
A crackling or hissing noise caused by electrical interference.
An oral dose of radioactive substance used in treatment and diagnosis of cancer.
example: Its most famous drink is the atomic cocktail—vodka, brandy, Champagne, splash of sherry.

definition: The explosion of an atomic bomb.
A nuclear reactor that uses controlled nuclear fission to generate energy.
etymology: From the fact that the first nuclear reactor, at the University of Chicago in 1942-1943, was literally constituted by a tall pile (heap) of graphite moderator blocks.

definition: A nuclear reactor that uses controlled nuclear fission to generate energy.
On, to, or at the top.
etymology: From a- (“on”) + top.

definition: Cause to be attached.
example: You need to attach the carabiner to your harness.
etymology: From Middle English attachen, from Old French atachier, variant of estachier (“bind”), derived from estache (“stick”), from Frankish *stakkā, *stakō (“stick”), from Proto-Germanic *stakô (“pole, bar, stick, stake”).

definition: Be present or associated with an event or entity.
example: Heart attacks are accompanied by destruction of heart tissue.

definition: A military submarine designed and armed to attack enemy shipping.
Someone who attacks.
etymology: From attack + -er.

definition: Disposed to attack.
etymology: From attack + -ing.

definition: To gain with effort.
example: To attain such a high level of proficiency requires hours of practice each day.
etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English atteinen, atteynen (“to achieve, attain; to be adequate or sufficient; to affect; to come or get to (a place), reach; to corrupt, taint; to overcome, overpower; to overtake;

definition: Achieved or reached.
example: The actual attained achievement test score.

definition: The act of being present (at a meeting or event etc.).
example: Attendance at the meeting is required.
etymology: From Middle English attendance, from Old French atendance, from atendre (“to attend, listen”).

definition: A call of students' names in a classroom.
Someone who waits on or tends to or attends to the needs of another.
example: Give your keys to the parking attendants and they will park your car for you.
etymology: From Middle English attendant, attendaunt, from Old French attendant. By surface analysis, attend + -ant.

definition: The process whereby a person concentrates on some features of the environment to the (relative) exclusion of others.
example: She's an attending in gastroenterology at Mass General.
etymology: From attend + -ing.

definition: Floor consisting of open space at the top of a house just below roof; often used for storage.
example: We went up to the attic to look for the boxes containing our childhood keepsakes.
etymology: From the practice of decorating the top storey of building facades in the Attic architectural style. From French attique, from Latin atticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀττικός (Attikós).

definition: A fan that blows heated air out of the attic of a building.
Direct toward itself or oneself by means of some psychological power or physical attributes.
example: Her good looks attract the stares of many men.
etymology: From Latin attractus, past participle of attrahere (“to draw to, attract”), from ad (“to”) + trahere (“to draw”).

definition: The force by which one object attracts another.
example: The Moon is held in its orbit by the attraction of the Earth's gravity.
etymology: From Middle English attraccioun, from Old French attraction, from Latin attractio from past participle of attrahō (= ad + trahō), equivalent to attract + -ion.

definition: A characteristic that provides pleasure and attracts.
example: Flowers are an attractor for bees.

definition: A construct whereby objects or individuals can be distinguished.
example: His finest attribute is his kindness.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin attributus.

definition: (of hair) colored a moderate reddish-brown.
example: Auburn hair.

definition: A variety of bridge in which tricks made in excess of the contract are scored toward game; now generally superseded by contract bridge.
etymology: From Latin auctiō (“an increase, auction”), from augere (“to increase”).

definition: A platform from which an auctioneer sells.
A variety of bridge in which tricks made in excess of the contract are scored toward game; now generally superseded by contract bridge.
example: Back then the game of choice around here was auction bridge.

definition: A firm that conducts auctions.
Sell at an auction.
The public sale of something to the highest bidder.
A dramatized, purely acoustic performance, broadcast on radio or published on audio media, such as tape or CD.
A computer file that contains digitized audio either in the Compact Disc (CDDA) format or in an MP3, AAC or other compressed format.
An audible acoustic wave frequency.
An audio library is a collection of sound recordings.
example: This is my own audio library.

definition: A recording of acoustic signals.
The area of a theater or concert hall where the audience sits.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin audītōrium, from audītōrius (“pertaining to hearing”). Equivalent to auditory + -ium.

definition: Added to or made greater in amount or number or strength.
example: His augmented renown.

definition: A sensation (as of a cold breeze or bright light) that precedes the onset of certain disorders such as a migraine attack or epileptic seizure.
example: This place has an aura of 19th century Paris.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin aura (“a breeze, a breath of air, the air”), from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra, “breeze, soft wind”), from ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”). Doublet of east, auster, air, and aria.

definition: The first light of day.
Undisputed credibility.
Endowed with authority.
example: An authoritative communique.

definition: Characteristic of an absolute ruler or absolute rule; having absolute sovereignty.
example: An authoritarian regime.
etymology: From authority + -arian, circa 1880.

definition: A government that concentrates political power in an authority not responsible to the people.
A government that concentrates political power in an authority not responsible to the people.
A document giving an official instruction or command.
example: I've got authorization. Call the office and you'll see.
etymology: From authorize + -ation.

definition: Endowed with authority.
example: An authoritative communique.

definition: An accessory for an automobile.
A factory where automobiles are manufactured.
Social control achieved as a manifestation of self-will or general consent.
A personal loan to purchase an automobile.
A race between (usually high-performance) automobiles.
The sport of racing automobiles.
Someone whose occupation is repairing and maintaining automobiles.
A biography of yourself.
