example: Elizabeth Millicent Leveson-Gower is 24th Countess of Sutherland; her son will be the 25th Earl.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman cuntesse, Old French contesse, from Latin comitissa; equivalent to count + -ess. Doublet of contessa.

definition: Rough and uncouth.
example: This childhood memory will take country-bred readers back to the days of their youth.

definition: The town or city that is the seat of government for a county.
A bond issued with detachable coupons that must be presented to the issuer for interest payments.
Possessing or displaying courage; able to face and deal with danger or fear without flinching.
example: A frank courageous heart … triumphed over pain.
etymology: From Middle English corajous, from Old French corageus, from corage + -eus.

definition: A person who carries a message.
etymology: From a convergence of Middle English corour, currour, from Old French coreor, agent noun of corir (“to run”), and Middle English courier, a borrowing of Middle French courrier, from Italian corriere.

definition: Court banner is formed by troops of the King.
Seek favor by fawning or flattery.
A plaster composed of isinglass on silk; formerly used to dress superficial wounds.
etymology: Originally applied as patches on the face by ladies at court.

definition: An ancient form of tennis played in a four-walled court.
A government building that houses the offices of a county government.
etymology: From court + house.

definition: A room in which a law court sits.
example: Television cameras were admitted in the courtroom.
etymology: From court + room.

definition: An area wholly or partly surrounded by walls or buildings.
example: The house was built around an inner court.
etymology: From court + yard.

definition: The child of your aunt or uncle.
etymology: From Middle English cosin germain, from Anglo-Norman cosin germain, cosine germaine. See also Middle English cosin, germain.

definition: A small inlet.
etymology: From Middle English cove, from Old English cofa (“chamber; den”), from Proto-West Germanic *kobō, from Proto-Germanic *kubô.

definition: A signed written agreement between two or more parties (nations) to perform some action.
etymology: From Middle English covenaunt, borrowed from Old French covenant (“agreement”), from Latin conveniēns, convenientem (“agreeing, agreeable, suitable, convenient”), present participle of conveniō (“to agree”).

definition: Crop planted to prevent soil erosion and provide green manure.
A small and very thin piece of glass used to cover the specimen on a microscope slide.
Fire that makes it difficult for the enemy to fire on your own individuals or formations.
example: Artillery provided covering fire for the withdrawal.

definition: A letter sent along with other documents to provide additional information.
A material used by builders to cover surfaces.
Secret or hidden; not openly practiced or engaged in or shown or avowed.
example: Covert actions by the CIA.
etymology: From Middle English covert, from Old French covert, past participle of covrir (“to cover”) (corresponding to Latin coopertus); cognate to cover.

definition: An intelligence operation so planned as to permit plausible denial by the sponsor.
A barn for cows.
Common water lily of eastern and central North America, having broad leaves and globe-shaped yellow flowers; in sluggish fresh or slightly brackish water.
A man who raises (or tends) cattle.
A light saddle horse trained for herding cattle.
A small town in a cattle-raising area of western North America.
A person who shows fear or timidity.
etymology: From Middle English coward, from Old French coart, cuard ( > French couard), from coue (“tail”), coe + -ard (pejorative agent noun suffix); coue, coe is in turn from Latin cauda.

definition: A boot with a high arch and fancy stitching; worn by American cowboys.
A hat with a wide brim and a soft crown; worn by American ranch hands.
Enjoying or affording comforting warmth and shelter especially in a small space.
example: A cozy nook near the fire.

definition: Ingratiate oneself to; often with insincere behavior.
Any of numerous varieties of crab apples cultivated for their small acidic (usually bright red) fruit used for preserves or as ornamentals for their blossoms.
A cocktail of cold cooked crabmeat and a sauce.
Grasses with creeping stems that root freely; a pest in lawns.
Legs of especially Alaska king crabs.
Someone skilled in shooting.
etymology: From crack (“excellent”) + shot.

definition: Large willow tree with stiff branches that are easily broken.
Grains of wheat that have been crushed into small pieces.
Hold gently and carefully.
example: He cradles the child in his arms.
etymology: From Middle English cradel, credel, from Old English cradol, from Proto-West Germanic *kradul, from Proto-Germanic *kradulaz, from Proto-Germanic *kradô (“(wicker) basket”). Related to cart.

definition: A fair at which objects made by craftsmen are offered for sale.
A labor union whose membership is restricted to workers in a particular craft.
Travel along a zigzag path.
example: Motorists had to crank their engine by hand.
etymology: From Dutch or Low German krank, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *krank, from Proto-Germanic *krangaz, *krankaz (“bent; weak”). Cognate with Scots crank, krank, German krank (“sick”).

definition: A hostile telephone call (from a crank).
Crank used to start an engine.
A hostile (usually anonymous) letter.
Produce in a routine or monotonous manner.
example: We have to crank out publications in order to receive funding.

definition: Start by cranking.
example: Crank up the engine.

definition: Playing craps.
Playing craps.
An emergency landing under circumstances where a normal landing is impossible (usually damaging the aircraft).
A rapid and intense course of training or research (usually undertaken in an emergency).
example: He took a crash course in Italian on his way to Italy.

definition: An intense desire for some particular thing.
etymology: From Middle English cravinge, from Old English crafing (“claim, demand”); equivalent to crave + -ing.

definition: Move slowly; in the case of people or animals with the body near the ground.
example: The crocodile was crawling along the riverbed.
etymology: Compare kraal.

definition: Prepare for sleep.
Low space beneath a floor of a building; gives workers access to wiring or plumbing.
A slow mode of locomotion on hands and knees or dragging the body.
example: A crawl was all that the injured man could manage.

definition: A point on the elbow where the ulnar nerve passes near the surface; a sharp tingling sensation results when the nerve is knocked against the bone.
Any of several leguminous plants of western North America causing locoism in livestock.
Soft unripened cheese made of sweet milk and cream.
example: Would you like some cream cheese in your sandwich?
etymology: Named for the cream from which the cheese was produced.

definition: A small pitcher for serving cream.
Puff filled with cream or custard.
example: To be in the cream puff.

definition: White sauce made with cream.
Leafy-stemmed violet of eastern North America having large white or creamy flowers faintly marked with purple.
Create mentally and abstractly rather than with one's hands.
A document attesting to the truth of certain stated facts.
Capable of being believed.
example: Completely credible testimony.
etymology: From Middle English credible, borrowed from Middle French credible, from Latin crēdibilis (“worthy of belief”), from crēdō (“believe”); see credit.

definition: A private firm that maintains consumer credit data files and provides credit information to authorized users for a fee.
The amount of money a bank has lent and may lose if it is not paid back.
example: The calculated expected maximum exposure value is not to be confused with the maximum credit exposure possible.

definition: An estimate, based on previous dealings, of a person's or an organization's ability to fulfill their financial commitments.
A list of acknowledgements of those who contributed to the creation of a film (usually run at the end of the film).
Any system of principles or beliefs.
example: A creed is a manifesto of religious or spiritual beliefs.

definition: A channel occupied (or formerly occupied) by a stream.
etymology: From creek + bed.

definition: Feed given to young animals isolated in a creep.
A slow mode of locomotion on hands and knees or dragging the body.
example: The traffic moved at a creep.
etymology: From Middle English crepynge, crepinde, crepende, crepande, from Old English crēopende, from Proto-Germanic *kreupandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *kreupaną (“to creep, crawl”), equivalent to creep + -ing.

definition: Resembling the new moon in shape.
etymology: The pronunciation with /z/ is a comparatively recent innovation due to the influence of words such as pheasant and present.

definition: Very rich flaky crescent-shaped roll.
Resembling the new moon in shape.
The top line of a hill, mountain, or wave.
etymology: From Middle English creste, from Old French creste (modern French crête) and perhaps continuing Old English cræsta (“crest, tuft, plume”); both ultimately from Vulgar Latin *cresta, from Latin crista. Doublet of crista.

definition: A plain straight neckline opening from shoulder to shoulder of sweaters.
The ball used in playing cricket.
Sports equipment used in playing cricket.
Either of two frogs with a clicking call.
A match between two cricket teams.
An act of disrespect that impedes the administration of justice.
(criminal law) an act punishable by law; usually considered an evil act.
(law) possession for which criminal sanctions are provided because the property may not lawfully be possessed or may not be possessed under certain circumstances.
Of a color at the end of the color spectrum (next to orange); resembling the color of blood or cherries or tomatoes or rubies.
etymology: PIE word *kʷŕ̥mis Late Middle English cremesyn, from obsolete French cramoisin or Old Spanish cremesín, from Arabic قِرْمِز (qirmiz), from Classical Persian کرمست (kirmist), from Middle Persian;

definition: Purple tinged with crimson.
Yellow tinged with crimson.
Disabled in the feet or legs.
example: A crippled soldier.

definition: (of something seen or heard) clearly defined.
example: The crisp snap of dry leaves underfoot.
etymology: Partly from the following: * Etymology 2 sense 1: crisp (adjective; see etymology 1). * Etymology 2 sense 2: Late Middle English crispen (“to curl;

definition: The smallest angle of incidence for which light is totally reflected.
The variant readings, footnotes, etc. found in a scholarly work or a critical edition of a text.
Find fault with; express criticism of; point out real or perceived flaws.
example: The paper criticized the new movie.
etymology: From critic + -ize; first element from Ancient Greek κριτικός (kritikós, “of or for judging, able to discern”), from κρίσις (krísis, “decision, judgement”).

definition: Having or marked by bends or angles; not straight or aligned.
example: Crooked country roads.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: Appear at the surface.
example: The peculiarities of the author are beginning to crop out.

definition: Appear suddenly or unexpectedly; happen unexpectedly.
example: We'll finish tonight if no problems crop up.

definition: Moderately sweet raised roll containing spices and raisins and citron and decorated with a cross-shaped sugar glaze.
Question closely, or question a witness that has already been questioned by the opposing side.
example: The witness was cross-examined by the defense.

definition: An infection that is acquired at a hospital or other healthcare facility.
Make the sign of the cross; in the Catholic religion.
Woody flowering vine of southern United States; stems show a cross in transverse section.
Either of two fine mutually perpendicular lines that cross in the focus plane of an optical instrument and are used for sighting or calibration.
example: He had the target in his cross hairs.

definition: Classification according to more than one attribute at the same time.
example: The cross-classification of cases was done by age and sex.

definition: (law) close questioning of a hostile witness in a court of law to discredit or throw a new light on the testimony already provided in direct examination.
etymology: From cross- + examination.

definition: Someone who questions a witness carefully (especially about testimony given earlier).
Relating to different languages.
example: Cross-linguistic evidence.
etymology: From cross- + linguistic.

definition: Refer from one entry to another, as in catalogues, books, and lists.
etymology: From cross- + refer.

definition: Shaped in the form of a cross.
Two stitches forming a cross or X.
etymology: From cross- + stitch.

definition: Strabismus in which one or both eyes turn inward toward the nose.
Someone who helps people (especially children) at a traffic crossing.
The interchange of sections between pairing homologous chromosomes during the prophase of meiosis.
A voter who is registered as a member of one political party but who votes in the primary of another party.
Any of several perennials of the genus Aletris having grasslike leaves and bitter roots reputed to cure colic.
Pungent Old World wild onion.
(architecture) a step on the top of a gable wall.
An emaciated horse likely soon to become carrion and so attractive to crows.
Having the approximate size of a crow.
Shrubby annual of the Mediterranean region with yellowish-white flowers.
A glass blown into a globe which is later flattened and spun to form a disk.
example: The convex half of an achromatic lens is composed of crown glass.
etymology: So called from a crown-like shape given to it in the process of blowing.

definition: The most desirable assets of a corporation.
example: Their crown jewels figured prominently in the takeover attempt.

definition: Regalia (jewelry and other paraphernalia) worn by a sovereign on state occasions.
example: The crown jewels in the United Kingdom are heavily guarded and anyone trying to steal them will certainly have a hard time.

definition: A male heir apparent to a throne.
The wife of a crown prince.
A roast of the rib section of lamb.
Having an (artificial) crown on a tooth.
example: Had many crowned teeth.
etymology: From Middle English coronede, crouned, crowned, crownyd, equivalent to crown + -ed. Piecewise doublet of coronaed.

definition: A nation's ruler or head of state usually by hereditary right.
A cruel act; a deliberate infliction of pain and suffering.
etymology: From Middle English cruelte, from Old French crualté (French cruauté), from Latin crudelitas. By surface analysis, cruel + -ty.

definition: Control mechanism for keeping an automobile at a set speed.
A passenger ship used commercially for pleasure cruises.
A passenger ship used commercially for pleasure cruises.
A car in which policemen cruise the streets; equipped with radiotelephonic communications to headquarters.
etymology: From cruise + -er.

definition: Make a crushing noise.
example: His shoes were crunching on the gravel.
etymology: From earlier craunch, cranch, of imitative origin.

definition: Exert oneself continuously, vigorously, or obtrusively to gain an end or engage in a crusade for a certain cause or person; be an advocate for.
example: She is crusading for women's rights.
etymology: From French croisade, introduced into English (in the French spelling) by 1575. The modern spelling emerges c. 1760,.

definition: Extinguish by crushing.
The outer layer of the Earth.
example: To earn one's crust.

definition: A glass or crystal globe used in crystal gazing by fortunetellers.
example: The psychic looked into the crystal ball and saw into the future.

definition: Transmitting light; able to be seen through with clarity.
example: The cold crystalline water of melted snow.
etymology: From Middle English cristal cleer. Emphatic form of clear in visual and metaphorical “understandable” senses. Compare clear as a bell (“very clear (of sound)”).

definition: A counter tube in which an ionizing event increases conductivity.
A detector consisting of a fine wire in contact with a galena crystal; acts as a rectifier.
A microphone in which sound waves vibrate a piezoelectric crystal that generates a varying voltage.
A microphone in which sound waves vibrate a piezoelectric crystal that generates a varying voltage.
A cartridge in which an output voltage is produced by the vibration of a piezoelectric crystal.
An early radio receiver using a crystal detector.
Evergreen shrub of eastern North America having white or creamy bell-shaped flowers and dark green hairy leaves used for tea during American Revolution.
A green crystal (violet in water) used as a dye or stain or bactericide or fungicide or anthelmintic or burn treatment.
The volume equal to a cube one foot on each side.
The volume equal to a cube one inch on each side.
A number that when multiplied three times equals a given number.
example: 3 is the cube root of 27.

definition: Shaped like a cube.
Involving the cube and no higher power of a quantity or variable.
example: A cubic equation.
etymology: From Middle French cubique, equivalent to cube + -ic.

definition: The volume equal to a cube one foot on each side.
The volume equal to a cube one inch on each side.
A metric unit of volume or capacity equal to 1000 liters.
An actor's line that immediately precedes and serves as a reminder for some action or speech.
etymology: From Middle English cu (used for half a farthing, from q as an abbreviation for Latin quadrāns (“quarter of an as”)), from Latin cū, kū. Compare French ku.

definition: Sports implement consisting of a tapering rod used to strike a cue ball in pool or billiards.
Hit with the hand.
example: Cuffing season.
etymology: From Middle English cuffe, coffe (“glove, mitten”), of obscure origin.

definition: Of or relating to or used in cooking.
example: Her culinary skills were excellent.
etymology: Borrowed from French culinaire, itself a borrowing from Latin culīnārius, from culīna (“kitchen”).

definition: The practice or manner of preparing food or the food so prepared.
(of land or fields) prepared for raising crops by plowing or fertilizing.
example: Cultivated land.

definition: Arable land that is worked by plowing and sowing and raising crops.
Plants that are grown for their produce.
Yields the staple food of 50 percent of world's population.
Socialization through training and education to develop one's mind or manners.
example: Her cultivation was remarkable.
etymology: From Medieval Latin cultivātus, perfect passive participle of cultivō, + -ion, or Middle French cultivation. By surface analysis, cultivate + -ion.

definition: The branch of anthropology that deals with human culture and society.
With regard to a culture.
example: Culturally integrated.
etymology: From cultural + -ly.

definition: A condition of disorientation affecting someone who is suddenly exposed to an unfamiliar culture or way of life or set of attitudes.
example: Having grown up in rural Arkansas, I experienced tremendous culture shock on moving to Harlem.
etymology: From the earlier form cultural shock.

definition: Increasing by successive addition.
example: The benefits are cumulative.
etymology: From cumulate + -ive. Compare also French cumulatif, Italian cumulativo and Spanish cumulativo.

definition: An election in which each person has as many votes as there are positions to be filled and they can all be cast for one candidate or can be distributed in any manner.
Any fungus that is a member of the subclass Discomycetes.
etymology: From cup + fungus, from its natural cup-like shape.

definition: Hook (usually on the underside of a shelf) for hanging cups.
The custodian of a collection (as a museum or library).
etymology: From Latin cūrātor (“one who has care of a thing, a manager, guardian, trustee”), from cūrāre (“to take care of”), from cūra (“care, heed, attention, anxiety, grief”).

definition: A horse's bit with an attached chain or strap to check the horse.
A stock market for trading in securities not listed on the New York Stock Exchange.
A roof with two or more slopes on each side of the ridge.
Service provided to customers who remain in their vehicles.
Freed from illness or injury.
example: The patient appears cured.

definition: Form a curl, curve, or kink.
example: The cigar smoke curled up at the ceiling.

definition: A piece of soft paper on which a lock of hair is rolled up for curling.
Shape one's body into a curl.
example: She curled farther down under the covers.

definition: (of hair) having curls or waves.
example: They envied her naturally curly hair.
etymology: From curl + -y.

definition: Rare small fern of northeastern North America having numerous slender spiraling fronds and forming dense tufts.
Shrubby clematis of the eastern United States having curly foliage.
A flow of electric charge.
An integrated course of academic studies.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin curriculum (“course”), derived from currō (“run, move quickly”). Doublet of curricle.

definition: A leaf from the curry tree, valued as seasoning in southern and west-coast Indian and Sri Lankan cooking.
example: In the absence of tulsi leaves, curry leaves are used for rituals, such as pujas.

definition: Pungent blend of cumin and ground coriander seed and turmeric and other spices.
Deserving a curse; sometimes used as an intensifier.
example: Villagers shun the area believing it to be cursed.
etymology: From Middle English cursed, cursd, curst, corsed, curset, cursyd, equivalent to curse + -ed.

definition: Burdened with.
A private lecture to a husband by his wife.
etymology: An allusion to the curtains that hung around old-fashioned beds.

definition: The first performance (as of a theatrical production).
The trace of a point whose direction of motion changes.
A mechanical damper; absorbs energy of sudden impulses.
Tall straggling shrub with large globose crimson-yellow flowers; western Australia.
Litigation to settle custody of the children of a divorced couple.
A legal action to determine custody (usually of children following a divorce).
Built for a particular individual.
In accordance with convention or custom.
example: Sealed the deal with the customary handshake.
etymology: From Middle English custumary, from Medieval Latin custumarius. By surface analysis, custom + -ary.

definition: An association of nations to promote free trade within the union and set common tariffs for nations that are not members.
Someone who cuts or carves stone.
The angle between the face of a cutting tool and the surface of the work.
The position of greatest importance or advancement; the leading position in any movement or field.
example: The company prides itself for staying at the cutting edge of technology.

definition: A cutting implement; a tool for cutting.
In accord with the most fashionable ideas or style.
example: Cutting-edge technology.

definition: An assault on electronic communication networks.
etymology: From cyber- + terrorism.

definition: A person who rides a bicycle.
etymology: From cycle + -ist, 1882.

definition: Believing the worst of human nature and motives; having a sneering disbelief in e.g. selflessness of others.
etymology: Originated 1542, from Classical Latin cynicus (“Cynic/cynic”, adjective) + -al. By surface analysis, cynic + -al. In reference to dogs, with allusion to the ultimate etymology (Ancient Greek κυνικός (kunikós, “doglike”)).

definition: A short knife with a pointed blade used for piercing or stabbing.
etymology: A wanderword relationship to Old Armenian դակու (daku, “adze, axe”) and the above set of words has also been suggested; a further connection to Ancient Greek θήγω (thḗgō, “to sharpen, whet”) is uncertain.

definition: Resembling a dagger.
Any of various bog plants of the genus Drosera having leaves covered with sticky hairs that trap and digest insects; cosmopolitan in distribution.
Any of numerous composite plants having flower heads with well-developed ray flowers usually arranged in a single whorl.
etymology: From Middle English dayesye, from Old English dæġes ēage (“daisy”, literally “day's eye”) due to the flowers closing their blossoms during night. The rhyming slang comes from daisy roots for boots.

definition: Any of various mostly Australian attractively shaped shrubs of the genus Olearia grown for their handsome and sometimes fragrant evergreen foliage and profusion of daisy flowers with white or purple or blue rays.
(figurative) a series of associated things or people or experiences.
etymology: The noun is derived from daisy + chain. The verb is derived from the noun.

definition: A wheel around which is a set of print characters that make a typing impression on paper.

Any of various mostly Australian attractively shaped shrubs of the genus Olearia grown for their handsome and sometimes fragrant evergreen foliage and profusion of daisy flowers with white or purple or blue rays.
Connect devices on a part of a chip or circuit board in a computer.
example: We daisy-chained several USB hubs to see if we could reach the far side of the room.
etymology: The verb is derived from daisy chain (noun).

definition: Obstruct with, or as if with, a dam.
example: Dam the gorges of the Yangtse River.

definition: Deaden (a sound or noise), especially by wrapping.
example: To damp cloth.
etymology: From Middle English dampen (“to stifle; suffocate”), from Old English damp, from Proto-Germanic *dampaz.

definition: A course of some impermeable material laid in the foundation walls of building near the ground to prevent dampness from rising into the building.
A lesson in dancing.
Large room used mainly for dancing.
One of a pair of people who dance together.
A professional teacher of dancing.
A dangerous area.
A wild and exciting undertaking (not necessarily lawful).
Disposed to venture or take risks.
example: The most daring of contemporary fiction writers.

definition: Bread made with whole wheat flour.
Chocolate liquor with cocoa butter and small amounts of sugar and vanilla; lecithin is usually added.
(plural) spectacles that are darkened or polarized to protect the eyes from the glare of the sun.
A lantern with a single opening and a sliding panel that can be closed to conceal the light.
Covered with dark hair.
Having a dark color.
Of a dark shade of grey.
Of a dark shade of grey.
Having hair of a dark color.
example: A dark-haired beauty.
etymology: From dark + haired.

definition: Naturally having skin of a dark color.
example: A dark-skinned beauty.

definition: Having dark spots.
Something of little value.
example: His opinion isn't worth a darn.
etymology: A minced oath of damn.

definition: A small narrow pointed missile that is thrown or shot.
example: Soon as I felt the floor tremor I made a dart for the door.
etymology: Compare Old High German tart (“javelin, dart”), Old English daroþ, dearod (“javelin, spear, dart”), Swedish dart (“dart, dagger”), Icelandic darraður, darr, dör (“dart, spear”).

definition: A circular board of wood or cork used as the target in the game of darts.
Someone who plays the game of darts.
Any of several small ungulate mammals of Africa and Asia with rodent-like incisors and feet with hooflike toes.
Conversion from one way of encoding data to another way.
(computer science) the encryption of data for security purposes.
An arrangement of data consisting of sets and subsets such that every subset of a set is of lower rank than the set.
Creation and maintenance of a database.
Tall tropical feather palm tree native to Syria bearing sweet edible fruit.
An Asiatic persimmon tree cultivated for its small yellow or purplish-black edible fruit much valued by Afghan tribes.
Earliest horse; extinct primitive dog-sized four-toed Eocene animal.
etymology: Calque of translingual Eohippus.

definition: Time during which clocks are set one hour ahead of local standard time; widely adopted during summer to provide extra daylight in the evenings.
Time during which clocks are set one hour ahead of local standard time; widely adopted during summer to provide extra daylight in the evenings.
Normal vision in daylight; vision with sufficient illumination that the cones are active and hue is perceived.
The time after sunrise and before sunset while it is light outside.
example: It is easier to make the repairs in the daytime.
etymology: From day + time.

definition: Existing in fact whether with lawful authority or not.
example: De facto segregation is as real as segregation imposed by law.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Latin dē factō (literally “according to fact”), from dē (“according to”) + ablative of factum (“fact, deed, act”).

definition: Reduce the emphasis.
etymology: From de- + emphasize.

definition: Something doomed to failure.
example: He finally admitted that the legislation was a dead duck.

definition: A metaphor that has occurred so often that it has become a new meaning of the expression (e.g., ‘he is a snake’ may once have been a metaphor but after years of use it has died and become a new sense of the word ‘snake’).
Social or verbal interchange (usually followed by ‘with’).
example: I've had dealings with Jo in the past, and found her very stubborn.

definition: Given out in portions.
An accounting entry acknowledging sums that are owing.
example: A cash sale is recorded as debit on the cash account and as credit on the sales account.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French debet, from Latin debitum (“what is owed, a debt”), neuter of debitus, past participle of debere (“to owe”); Doublet of debt.

definition: An account balance in which debits exceed credits, and the customer owes the bank money.
A card (usually plastic) that enables the holder to withdraw money or to have the cost of purchases charged directly to the holder's bank account.
An accounting entry acknowledging sums that are owing.
Account of payments owed; usually the left side of a financial statement.
The sudden spread of dust and debris from a collapsing building.
example: The destruction of the building produced an enormous debris surge.

definition: A written promise to repay a debt.
The maximum borrowing power of a governmental entity.
A measure of a company's total debt to its total assets.
example: A debt ratio indicates how risky it would be for a bank to extend a loan to a company, with a higher ratio indicating great risk.

definition: (astronomy) the angular distance of a celestial body north or to the south of the celestial equator; expressed in degrees; used with right ascension to specify positions on the celestial sphere.
The quality of conforming to standards of propriety and morality.
etymology: From Latin decentia, from decens. Equivalent to decent + -cy. Compare French décence.

definition: A misleading falsehood.
example: Deliberate deception.
etymology: From Middle English decepcioun, from Old French decepcion, from Latin dēcipiō (“to deceive”).

definition: Someone who administers a business.
A point or fact or remark that settles something conclusively.
A folding chair for use outdoors; a wooden frame supports a length of canvas.
A superstructure on the upper deck of a ship.
A statement that is emphatic and explicit (spoken or written).
etymology: From Middle English declaration, declaracion, declaracioun, from Old French declaration (French déclaration), from Latin dēclārātiōnem, accusative of Latin dēclārātiō.

definition: Decoration consisting of the layout and furnishings of a livable interior.
example: Her living room had a lush Persian-style decor.

definition: Becoming less or smaller.
etymology: From decrease + -ing (participial suffix).

definition: Give entirely to a specific person, activity, or cause.

etymology: From Middle French transcription, or directly from Latin transcriptiōnem, from trānscrībō (“transcribe”).

definition: A public expenditure (as for unemployment compensation or veteran's benefits) that is not for goods and services.
A possession whose ownership changes or lapses.
A qualitative change.
example: Undergo a radical transformation.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English transformacioun, from Middle French, from Ecclesiastical Latin trānsfōrmātiō. Morphologically transform + -ation.

definition: A gene that disposes normal cells to change into cancerous tumor cells.
A line providing public transit.
Of or relating to or characterized by transition.
example: Adolescence is a transitional stage between childhood and adulthood.
etymology: From transition + -al.

definition: A written communication in a second language having the same meaning as the written communication in a first language.
example: This old text needs translation into modern English before it is published.
etymology: From Middle English translacioun (“transfer, translation”), from Anglo-Norman translacioun, from Latin trānslātiō, from trānslāt-, the supine stem of trānsferō (“to transfer, transport, transform, translate”).

definition: A person who translates written messages from one language to another.
A path over which electrical signals can pass.
A conductor for transmitting electrical or optical signals or electric power.
Rotating shaft that transmits rotary motion from the engine to the differential.
The gears that transmit power from an automobile engine via the driveshaft to the live axle.
The coordinated universal time when a transmission is sent from Earth to a spacecraft or other celestial body.
Transfer to another.
example: A Mayday call was transmitted by the stricken vessel.
etymology: From Middle English transmitten, borrowed from Latin trānsmittō (“transmit”, verb, literally “across-send”).

definition: Someone who transmits a message.
etymology: From transmit + -er.

definition: A gemstone having the property of transmitting light without serious diffusion.
A clear quartz used in making electronic and optical equipment.
Lift and reset in another soil or situation.
example: Transplant the young rice plants.
etymology: From Middle English transplaunten, from Old French transplanter, from Late Latin transplantare, equivalent to trans- + plant.

definition: (American football) an illegal block.
A hinged or sliding door in a floor or ceiling.
A line or series of traps.
(American football) a play in which a defensive player is allowed to cross the line of scrimmage and then blocked off as the runner goes through the place the lineman vacated.
The collection and removal of garbage.
An accumulation of refuse and discarded matter.
The collection and removal of garbage.
Any physical damage to the body caused by violence or accident or fracture etc.; the condition of an injury.
example: Mild trauma; major trauma.
etymology: From Ancient Greek τραῦμα (traûma, “wound, damage”).

definition: Of or relating to a physical injury or wound to the body.
etymology: From the Latin [medicāmentum] traumaticum, from traumaticus.

definition: (frequently plural) expenses incurred by an employee in the performance of the job and usually reimbursed by the employer.
A kit for carrying toilet articles while traveling.
Move very fast.
Soiled from travel.
example: Travel-soiled clothes.

definition: Tired by travel.
A person who changes location.
etymology: From travel + -er.

definition: The act of going from one place to another.
example: He enjoyed selling but he hated the travel.
etymology: From travel + -ing.

definition: A portable rectangular container for carrying clothes.
A salesman who travels to call on customers.
A wave in which the medium moves in the direction of propagation of the wave.
The act of going from one place to another.
example: He enjoyed selling but he hated the travel.

definition: A salesman who travels to call on customers.
An open receptacle for holding or displaying or serving articles or food.
etymology: From Middle English trey, from Old English trēġ, trīġ (“wooden board, tray”), from Proto-West Germanic *trauwi, from Proto-Germanic *trawją (“wooden vessel”), from Proto-Indo-European *drewo-, *dóru (“tree; wood”).

definition: Table linen consisting of a small cloth for a tray.
Put down or press the foot, place the foot.
example: For fools rush in where angels fear to tread.
etymology: From Middle English treden, from Old English tredan, from Proto-West Germanic *tredan, from Proto-Germanic *trudaną.

definition: Walk on and flatten.
Place or press the foot on.
A storehouse for treasures.
etymology: From Middle English tresour-hous, equivalent to treasure + house.

definition: A 16th-century ship loaded with treasure.
etymology: Calque of Chinese 寶船 /宝船 (bǎochuán).

definition: A special law-enforcement agent of the United States Treasury.
Stock that has been bought back by the issuing corporation and is available for retirement or resale; it is issued but not outstanding; it cannot vote and pays no dividends.
Any of the main branches arising from the trunk or a bough of a tree.
Small bushy tree grown on islands of the Caribbean and off the Atlantic coast of the southern United States; yields cotton with unusually long silky fibers.
Pale arboreal American cricket noted for loud stridulation.
The tending of and caring for trees.
Gaunt Tasmanian evergreen shrubby tree with slender tapering leaves 3 to 5 feet long.
A climbing lizard of western United States and northern Mexico.
Evergreen shrub of southwestern United States and Mexico often cultivated for its fragrant golden yellow flowers.
Any typical arboreal squirrel.
Evergreen South American shrub naturalized in United States; occasionally responsible for poisoning livestock.
Resembling a tree in form and branching structure.
The worship of trees.
Impinge or infringe upon.
example: This matter entrenches on other domains.
etymology: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French trenche. Doublet of tranche and traunch. Possible doublet of English: truncate

definition: A military style raincoat; belted with deep pockets.
Marked by pain in muscles and joints and transmitted by lice.
Resembling frostbite but without freezing; resulting from exposure to cold and wet.
etymology: From its prevalence during the trench warfare of World War I.

definition: A knife with a double-edged blade for hand-to-hand fighting.
An acute communicable infection of the respiratory tract and mouth marked by ulceration of the mucous membrane.
etymology: Probably coined during World War I when the disease was common among soldiers in the trenches during trench warfare.

definition: A struggle (usually prolonged) between competing entities in which neither side is able to win.
Analysis of changes over time.
The initiating or popularizing of a trend or fashion.
Initiating or popularizing a trend.
A chad that is incompletely removed and still attached at three corners.
(printing) an impression made to check for errors.
(ancient Rome) an official elected by the plebeians to protect their interests.
example: The new magazine's goal is to give a tribune to unmarried mothers.
etymology: From Middle English tribune, from Old French tribun, tribune, from Latin tribunus (“tribune, tribal leader”), from tribus (“tribe”).

definition: Concept album compiling a performer's work or work supporting some worthy cause.
Put in motion or move to act.
example: Trigger a reaction.

definition: A very large indefinite number (usually hyperbole).
etymology: Borrowed from French trillion, from French tri- (“three”) + -illion, equivalent to tri- + -illion.

definition: A small military force that serves as a first line of defense; if they become engaged in hostilities it will trigger the intervention of stronger military forces.
Fresh soft French cheese containing at least 72% fat.
(horse racing) a title won by a horse that can win the Kentucky Derby and the Belmont Stakes and the Preakness.
An athletic contest in which a competitor must perform successively a hop and a step and a jump in continuous movement.
The act of getting three players out on one play.
example: There has only been one unassisted triple play recorded in the World Series.

definition: Musical time with three beats in each bar.
etymology: From triple + time (“measure, tempo”).

definition: Type with two empty spaces between lines.
Characterized by a buoyant rhythm.
example: A tripping singing measure.

definition: (informal) small and of little importance.
etymology: PIE word *tréyes * From Latin triviālis (“appropriate to the street-corner, commonplace, vulgar”), from trivium (“place where three roads meet”). Compare trivium, trivia.

definition: A group of soldiers.
example: 2022, CNN, First Russian troop to speak out publicly against Putin’s war. Hear what he has to say (archived).
etymology: Attested in English since 1545, from French troupe, from Back-formation from troupeau, from Middle French trope, troupe, from Old French trope, trupe, of unknown origin. Compare Early Medieval Latin troppus.

definition: Any land or sea or air vehicle designed to carry troops.
Movement of military units to a new location.
Any land or sea or air vehicle designed to carry troops.
A case in which to display trophies.
A husband who is an attractive young man; seldom the first husband of an affluent older woman.
etymology: By analogy with trophy wife.

definition: Relating to or situated in or characteristic of the tropics (the region on either side of the equator).
example: Tropical islands.
etymology: From tropic + -al.

definition: Leishmaniasis of the skin; characterized by ulcerative skin lesions.
The time for the earth to make one revolution around the sun, measured between two vernal equinoxes.
Someone who deliberately stirs up trouble.
Take the trouble to do something; concern oneself.
example: He did not trouble to call his mother on her birthday.

definition: Causing distress or worry or anxiety.
example: A new and troubling thought.

definition: (usually in the plural) a garment extending from the waist to the knee or ankle, covering each leg separately.
example: He had a sharp crease in his trousers.

definition: Flesh of any of several primarily freshwater game and food fishes.
etymology: From Middle English troute, troughte, trught, trouȝt, trouhte, partly from Old English truht (“trout”), and partly from Old French truite;

definition: Eastern North American dogtooth having solitary yellow flowers marked with brown or purple and spotted interiors.
Someone who drives a truck as an occupation.
A farm where vegetables are grown for market.
etymology: From truck (“to trade”).

definition: A large group of bacteria having rigid cell walls; motile types have flagella.
The true blackberry of Europe as well as any of numerous varieties having sweet edible black or dark purple berries.
Any of various insects of the order Hemiptera and especially of the suborder Heteroptera.
Any cedar of the genus Cedrus.
Any of numerous fungi of the division Eumycota.
Any plant of the genus Erica.
A climbing deciduous shrub with fragrant white or yellow or red flowers used in perfume and to flavor tea.
Small Mediterranean evergreen tree with small blackish berries and glossy aromatic leaves used for flavoring in cooking; also used by ancient Greeks to crown victors.
Large edible marine crustaceans having large pincers on the first pair of legs.
Any of various shrubby vines of the genus Piper.
One of the first seven ribs in a human being which attach to the sternum.
Any of several seals lacking external ear flaps and having a stiff hairlike coat with hind limbs reduced to swimming flippers.
Mexican evergreen climbing plant having large solitary funnel-shaped fragrant yellow flowers with purple-brown ridges in the throat.
The section of a band or orchestra that plays trumpets or cornets.
Tropical American tree with large peltate leaves and hollow stems.
North American herb having whorled leaves and terminal clusters of flowers spotted with purple.
Resembling the sound of a trumpet.
Shaped in the form of a trumpet.
example: Trumpet-shaped flowers.

definition: Tropical American tree with large peltate leaves and hollow stems.
Puffed breeches of the 16th and 17th centuries usually worn over hose.
Hinged lid for a trunk.
A written instrument legally conveying property to a trustee often used to secure an obligation such as a mortgage or promissory note.
A person (or institution) to whom legal title to property is entrusted to use for another's benefit.
etymology: From trust + -ee.

definition: A savings account deposited by someone who makes themselves the trustee for a beneficiary and who controls it during their lifetime; afterward the balance is payable to the previously named beneficiary.
Inclined to believe or confide readily; full of trust.
example: Great brown eye, true and trustful.
etymology: From Middle English trustyng, trostinge, tristynge, equivalent to trust + -ing.

definition: Worthy of trust or belief.
example: A trustworthy report.
etymology: From trust + -worthy.

definition: An intravenous anesthetic drug that has a hypnotic effect; induces relaxation and weakens inhibitions; is believed to induce people to talk freely.
A cataclysm resulting from a destructive sea wave caused by an earthquake or volcanic eruption.
example: A colossal tsunami destroyed the Minoan civilization in minutes.
etymology: Borrowed from Japanese 津波 (tsunami), from 津 (tsu, “harbour”) + 波 (nami, “wave”).

definition: A cart with an underslung axle and two seats.
Conduit consisting of a long hollow object (usually cylindrical) used to hold and conduct objects or liquids or gases.
example: A tube of toothpaste.
etymology: From Middle French tube, from Latin tubus (“tube, pipe”), related to tuba (“long trumpet; war-trumpet”), of obscure ultimate origin, but possibly connected to tībia (“shinbone, reed-pipe”); see there. Doublet of tubus.

definition: Tentacular tubular process of most echinoderms (starfish and sea urchins and holothurians) having a sucker at the end and used for e.g. locomotion and respiration.
A well made by driving a tube into the earth to a stratum that bears water.
Infection transmitted by inhalation or ingestion of tubercle bacilli and manifested in fever and small lesions (usually in the lungs but in various other parts of the body in acute stages).
Eatables (especially sweets).
etymology: From Old French estoc (“rapier”), from Italian stocco (“a truncheon, a short sword”). Doublet of estoc.

definition: Eat up; usually refers to a considerable quantity of food.
example: My son tucked in a whole pizza.

definition: A box for storing eatables (especially at boarding school).
Eat up; usually refers to a considerable quantity of food.
example: My son tucked in a whole pizza.
etymology: See tuck (1).

definition: A candy store in Great Britain.
etymology: From tuck (“snack food”) + shop.

definition: Having tucked or being tucked.
example: Tightly tucked blankets.

definition: A sewer who tucks.
etymology: From tuck + -er.

definition: Wear out completely.
A bag used for carrying food.
example: The swagman filled his tuckerbag.

definition: Pull hard.
example: The prisoner tugged at the chains.
etymology: From Middle English tuggen, from Old English togian (“to tow”), from Proto-West Germanic *togōn, from Proto-Germanic *tugōną (“to draw, pull”), from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to draw, pull; to lead”).

definition: Tropical American prickly pear of Jamaica.
etymology: Acronym of turnt up nonaffiliate.

definition: Important warm-water fatty fish of the genus Thunnus of the family Scombridae; usually served as steaks.
An oil obtained from tuna.
Salad composed primarily of chopped canned tuna fish.
Regulate (a radio or television set) in order to receive a certain station or program.
Adjust for (better) functioning.
example: Tune the engine.

definition: (music) calibrating something (an instrument or electronic circuit) to a standard frequency.
A metal implement with two prongs that gives a fixed tone when struck; used to tune musical instruments.
A passageway through or under something, usually underground (especially one for trains or cars).
example: The tunnel reduced congestion at that intersection.
etymology: From Middle English tonnel, from Old French tonel(e), diminutive of tone (“cask”), a word of uncertain origin and affiliation. Related to Old English tunne (“tun; cask; barrel”). More at tun.

definition: Rotary engine in which the kinetic energy of a moving fluid is converted into mechanical energy by causing a bladed rotor to rotate.
etymology: Borrowed from French turbine, from Latin turbō, turbinem (“tornado, whirlwind; crowd”).

definition: Unstable flow of a liquid or gas.
etymology: From Middle English turbulence (“turbidity, cloudiness”), from Late Latin turbulentia (“trouble, disquiet”). By surface analysis, turbulent + -ence.

definition: Surface layer of ground containing a mat of grass and grass roots.
example: In climates where grass struggles to grow, turf is usually used instead on sports fields.

definition: Put out or expel from a place.
A bitter struggle for territory or power or control or rights.
example: A turf war erupted between street gangs.
etymology: The phrase may have originated as a reference to the game of American football where two teams confront each other on a field of grass or turf.

definition: The lower joint of the leg of a turkey.
The wing of a turkey.
A violent disturbance.
etymology: Unknown. First appears c. 1526. Perhaps from Old French tremouille (“the hopper of a mill”).

definition: Flee; take to one's heels; cut and run.
The group that gathers together for a particular occasion.
example: A large turnout for the meeting.
etymology: Deverbal from turn out.

definition: The ratio of the number of workers that had to be replaced in a given time period to the average number of workers.
example: The company had an annual turnover of $500,000.
etymology: Deverbal from turn over.

definition: The ratio of the number of workers that had to be replaced in a given time period to the average number of workers.
Black-seeded bean of South America; usually dried.
Soup usually made of the flesh of green turtles.
Be a tutor to someone; give individual instruction.
example: She tutored me in Spanish.
etymology: From Middle English tutour, from Old French tuteur (French tuteur), from Latin tūtor (“a watcher, protector, guardian”), from tueor (“protect”); see tuition.

definition: An announcer on television.
Monitor used in a studio for monitoring the program being broadcast.
An omnidirectional antenna tuned to the broadcast frequencies assigned to television.
Position 12 in a countable series of things.
example: A twelfth of 240 is 20.
etymology: From Middle English twelfthe, twelfte, from Old English twelfta (“twelfth”), from Proto-Germanic *twaliftô (“twelfth”), equivalent to twelve + -th (ordinal suffix).

definition: One part in twelve equal parts.
The century from 1901 to 2000.
Coming next after the twenty-sixth in position.
etymology: From twenty-seven + -th (ordinal suffix).

definition: Coming next after the twenty-fifth in position.
etymology: From twenty-six + -th (ordinal suffix).

definition: Normal visual acuity, as measured by the ability to read charts at a distance of 20 feet.
etymology: From a method of testing vision by reading charts at a distance of 20 feet.

definition: The ability to see in reduced illumination (as in moonlight).
The lowest level of the ocean to which light can reach.
example: Oh, I can't talk right now, Duke. I'm in the twilight zone.
etymology: Because such a zone (in the literal sense of the term) is twilit; see twilight § Etymology.

definition: One of a pair of identical beds.
Two games instead of one (especially in baseball when the same two teams play two games on the same day).
A propeller plane with an engine that drives two propellers in opposite directions (for stability).
Practice sophistry; change the meaning of or be vague about in order to mislead or deceive.
example: Don't twist my words.

definition: A bit or drill having deep helical grooves.
A song associated with the dance ‘The Twist’ and the associated cultural craze.
example: There was Twist merchandise and memorabilia sold in those times, and many other music artists recorded twist songs.

definition: Vigorous deciduous European treelike shrub common along waysides; red berries turn black.
Make an uncontrolled, short, jerky motion.
example: His face is twitching.
etymology: From Middle English twicchen, from Old English *twiċċan, from Proto-West Germanic *twikkijan (“to nail, pin, fasten, clasp, pinch”).

definition: The cardinal number that is the sum of twenty-three and one.
A game in which a pitcher allows the opposing team only 2 hits.
Not faithful to a spouse or lover.
example: A two-timing boyfriend.

definition: The act of tying or binding things together.
etymology: From Middle English tiȝing, teing, from Old English *tīgung, tīging (“connection”), from Proto-Germanic *taugungō, from *taugijaną from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to tug, draw”). Equivalent to tie + -ing.

definition: An agreement by a party to sell one product but only on the condition that the buyer also purchases a different (or tied), usually unrelated product.
example: In recent years, changing business practices surrounding new technologies have put the legality of tying arrangements to the test.

definition: The act of securing an arriving vessel with ropes.
(biology) genus from which the name of a family or subfamily is formed; it is not necessarily the most representative genus but often the largest or best known or earliest described.
The original specimen from which the description of a new species is made.
A group of typists who can work for different persons.
A form of government in which the ruler is an absolute dictator (not restricted by a constitution or laws or opposition etc.).
etymology: Inherited from Middle English tirannye, from Old French tyrannie, from Medieval Latin tyrannia, tyrania, from Ancient Greek τυραννία (turannía, “tyranny”), from τύραννος (túrannos, “lord, master, sovereign, tyrant”).

definition: Hoop that covers a wheel.
etymology: Attested in the sense “rim of a wheel” since ca. 1500. Generally considered to be a use of Middle English tir(e), a clipped byform of atir (“equipment, furnishings, ornament”), whence modern attire.

definition: Very ugly.
Loose long overcoat of heavy fabric; usually belted.
example: Off slipped a sodden ulster. He hung it up angrily upon a peg ….
etymology: Named after the Ulster Overcoat Company of Belfast, Northern Ireland (Ulster), the original maker of this type of coat.

definition: Very high frequency sound; used in ultrasonography.
etymology: From ultra- + sound.

definition: Medium-sized two-needled pine of southern Europe having a spreading crown; widely cultivated for its sweet seeds that resemble almonds.
A small tent with a single supporting pole and radiating metal ribs.
Shaped in the form of an umbrella.
In complete agreement.
example: A unanimous decision.
etymology: From Latin ūnanimus (“of one mind”), from ūnus (“one”) + animus (“mind”). Displaced native Old English ānmōd (literally “one-minded”).

definition: Of one mind; without dissent.
example: The Senate unanimously approved the bill.
etymology: From unanimous + -ly.

definition: (used of persons or the military) not having or using arms.
example: Went alone and unarmed.
etymology: From un- + armed.

definition: Not endowed with authority.
etymology: From un- + authorized.

definition: Unauthorized military absence.
Not available or accessible or at hand.
example: Fresh milk was unavailable during the emergency.
etymology: From un- + available.

definition: Not made or become different.
example: The causes that produced them have remained unchanged.
etymology: From un- + changed.

definition: Conducive to or feeling mental discomfort.
example: This kind of life can prove disruptive and uncomfortable.
etymology: From un- + comfortable.

definition: Not consistent with or according to a constitution; contrary to the U.S. Constitution.
example: That recently passed political bill has been declared unconstitutional.
etymology: From un- + constitutional.

definition: Not covered with clothing.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: Victorious.
example: Undefeated in battle.
etymology: From un- + defeated.

definition: Kept secret.
example: The plan was kept carefully under wraps.

definition: Conducted with or marked by hidden aims or methods.
example: An undercover investigation.
etymology: From under + cover.

definition: (military) a secret agent hired by a state to obtain information about its enemies or by a business to obtain industrial secrets from competitors.
An operation involving secret work within a community or institution.
The act of keeping a secret watch for intelligence purposes.
Assign too low a value to.
example: Don't underestimate the value of this heirloom-you may sell it at a good price.
etymology: From under- + estimate.

definition: Under the level of the ground.
example: Underground caverns.
etymology: From Middle English undergrounde (adverb), equivalent to under + ground or under- + ground. Compare Dutch ondergrond, ondergronds, German Untergrund, Danish undergrunds.

definition: A system of clandestine printing and distribution of dissident or banned literature.
In the nature of something though not readily apparent.
example: An underlying meaning.
etymology: By surface analysis, underlie + -ing.

definition: Destroy property or hinder normal operations.
example: The war efforts were undermined by the constant bickering between the allies.
etymology: From under- + mine.

definition: Capable of being apprehended or understood.
etymology: From Middle English understondable, equivalent to understand + -able.

definition: Enter upon an activity or enterprise.
etymology: From Middle English undertaken; equivalent to under- + take (after undernim).

definition: Any piece of work that is undertaken or attempted.
example: He prepared for great undertakings.
etymology: By surface analysis, undertake + -ing.

definition: Cancel, annul, or reverse an action or its effect.
example: I wish I could undo my actions.
etymology: From Middle English undōn, from Old English ondōn, from Proto-West Germanic *andadōn (“to undo”), equivalent to un- + do. Cognate with West Frisian ûndwaan, ûntdwaan (“to undo; rid”), Dutch ontdoen (“to undo”).

definition: A queue of people waiting for employment.
The percentage of the work force that is unemployed at any given date.
Not even or uniform as e.g. in shape or texture.
example: An uneven color.
etymology: From Middle English uneven, from Old English unefen (“unequal, unlike, dissimilar, diverse, irregular”), equivalent to un- + even.

definition: A pair of parallel bars set at different heights; used in women's gymnastics.
Not expected or anticipated.
example: Unexpected guests.
etymology: From un- + expected.

definition: In a way that was not expected.
etymology: From unexpected + -ly or un- + expectedly.

definition: Not known or well known.
example: A name unfamiliar to most.
etymology: From un- + familiar.

definition: Having little or no knowledge of.
Not brought to the desired final state.
example: Unfinished business.
etymology: From un- + finished.

definition: Work that is left incomplete.
Below the required standards for a purpose.
example: An unfit parent.
etymology: From un- + fit.

definition: Not favored by fortune; marked or accompanied by or resulting in ill fortune.
example: An unfortunate turn of events.
etymology: From un- + fortunate, doublet of infortunate.

definition: A person who suffers misfortune.
Not in or exhibiting good health in body or mind.
example: Unhealthy ulcers.
etymology: From un- + healthy.

definition: An imaginary creature represented as a white horse with a long horn growing from its forehead.
Not yet identified.
example: An unidentified species.
etymology: From un- + identified.

definition: A type of motion in which the velocity of an object changes by an equal amount in every equal time period.
So as to be unique.
example: He could determine uniquely the properties of the compound.
etymology: From unique + -ly.

definition: Someone authorized to transact every kind of business for the principal.
Coupling that connects two rotating shafts allowing freedom of movement in all directions.
example: In motor vehicles a universal joint allows the driveshaft to move up and down as the vehicle passes over bumps.

definition: (logic) a proposition that asserts something of all members of a class.

Membrane initially completely investing the young sporophore of various mushrooms that is ruptured by growth; represented in the mature mushroom by a volva around lower part of stem and scales on upper surface of the cap.
In every case.
example: People universally agree on this.
etymology: From Middle English universally; equivalent to universal + -ly.

definition: Not conforming to legality, moral law, or social convention.
example: He was charged with unlawful use of a car.
etymology: From Middle English unlawful; equivalent to un- + lawful.

definition: Having no limits in range or scope.
example: To start with a theory of unlimited freedom is to end up with unlimited despotism.
etymology: From Middle English unlimitid, equivalent to un- + limited.

definition: Not firmly fastened or secured.
example: An unlocked room.

definition: Having or bringing misfortune.
example: Friday the 13th is an unlucky date.
etymology: From un- + lucky.

definition: Being or having an unknown or unnamed source.
example: An unnamed donor.

definition: Not necessary.
example: The automatic child-frightener made clowns unnecessary.
etymology: From un- + necessary.

definition: Not having official authority or sanction.
example: A sort of unofficial mayor.
etymology: From un- + official.

definition: Not paid.
example: Unpaid wages.
etymology: From un- + paid.

definition: A person who performs voluntary work.
A person who is not pleasant or agreeable.
Regarded with disfavor or lacking general approval.
example: Unpopular ideas.
etymology: From un- + popular.

definition: Not capable of being foretold.
etymology: From un- + predictable.

definition: Lacking in reality or substance or genuineness; not corresponding to acknowledged facts or criteria.
example: Ghosts and other unreal entities.
etymology: From un- + real.

definition: Not realistic.
example: Unrealistic expectations.
etymology: From un- + realistic.

definition: Not reasonable; not showing good judgment.
etymology: From Middle English unresonable, equivalent to un- + reasonable, originally partly after Latin irratiōnābilis.

definition: Liable to be erroneous or misleading.
etymology: From un- + reliable.

definition: Lacking in security or safety.
etymology: From un- (not) + safe.

definition: Not seen or perceived.
example: Unseen natural resources.
etymology: From Middle English unsen, unseyn, unseien, from Old English unġesewen, from Proto-Germanic *unsewanaz, equivalent to un- + seen.

definition: Not successful; having failed or having an unfavorable outcome.
example: His unsuccessful attempt earned him sympathy, condolences, and an occasional good-natured ribbing.
etymology: From un- + successful.

definition: A person with a record of failing; someone who loses consistently.
Lacking self-confidence.
example: A very unsure young man.
etymology: From Middle English unsure, equivalent to un- + sure. Piecewise doublet of insecure and unsecure.

definition: Not yet used or soiled.
example: An unused envelope.
etymology: From un- + used.

definition: Infrequently exposed to.
example: Feet unused to shoes.

definition: To a remarkable degree or extent.
example: She was unusually tall.
etymology: From unusual + -ly or un- + usually.

definition: Revealed; especially by having a veil removed.
example: A new generation of unveiled women in Iran.
etymology: From Middle English unveiled, vnueylyd, equivalent to un- + veil + -ed.

definition: Not wanted; not needed.
example: Tried to give away unwanted kittens.
etymology: From un- + wanted.

definition: Not disposed to and refusing to do something.
example: Unwilling to face facts.
etymology: From un- + willing.

definition: A contented state of being happy and healthy and prosperous.
example: The town was finally on the upbeat after our recent troubles.
etymology: From up- + beat.

definition: The act of changing something to bring it up to date (usually by adding something).
example: Criminal records need regular updating.

definition: Keep or maintain in unaltered condition; cause to remain or last.
etymology: From Middle English upholden, equivalent to up- + hold. Compare Dutch ophouden (“to stop, cease, hold up”), German aufhalten (“to stop, halt, detain”).

definition: Rearmost or uppermost area in the balcony containing the least expensive seats.
(mathematics) a number equal to or greater than any other number in a given set.
A higher deck.
The upper part of the mantle.
In a vertical position; not sloping.
example: An upright post.
etymology: From Middle English upright, uppryght, upriht, from Old English upriht (“upright; erect”), from Proto-Germanic *upprehtaz, equivalent to up- + right.

definition: A piano with a vertical sounding board.
Organized opposition to authority; a conflict in which one faction tries to wrest control from another.
etymology: By surface analysis, uprise + -ing.

definition: A disorder of digestive function characterized by discomfort or heartburn or nausea.
Causing an emotional disturbance.
example: An upsetting experience.

definition: In the direction against a stream's current.
example: Input entry is upstream of input validation in the runtime process.
etymology: From up- + stream.

definition: Directed up.
example: The cards were face upward.
etymology: From Old English upweardes, equivalent to up + -ward.

definition: Spatially or metaphorically from a lower to a higher position.
example: The fragments flew upwards.
etymology: From Middle English upwardes, from Old English upweardes, equivalent to up + -wards. Cognate with Dutch opwaarts (“upwards”), German aufwärts (“upwards”).

definition: Any ore from which uranium can be extracted.
A story that appears mysteriously and spreads spontaneously in various forms and is usually false; contains elements of humor or horror and is popularly believed to be true.
The clearing and rebuilding and redevelopment of urban slums.
Spur on or encourage especially by cheers and shouts.
A verbalization that encourages you to attempt something.
Capable of being put to use.
example: Usable byproducts.
etymology: From Old French usable, from the verb user (“to use”).

definition: Easy to use.
Be a precursor of.
example: The fall of the Berlin Wall ushered in the post-Cold War period.

definition: End one's encounter with somebody by causing or permitting the person to leave.
A bond issued to finance the construction of public utility services.
A male baseball player valued for the ability to play at several positions.
A baseball player valued for the ability to play at several positions.
(computer science) a program designed for general support of the processes of a computer.
example: A computer system provides utility programs to perform the tasks needed by most users.

definition: A female baseball player valued for the ability to play at several positions.
Used of beef; usable but inferior.
The act of using.
example: Skilled in the utilization of computers.
etymology: From French utilisation or from utilize + -ation.

definition: Put into service; make work or employ for a particular purpose or for its inherent or natural purpose.
example: How do you utilize this tool?
etymology: From French utiliser, from Italian utilizzare, from utile (“useful”), from Latin ūtilis, from ūtī (“use”).

definition: Of the greatest possible degree or extent or intensity.
example: Utmost contempt.
etymology: PIE word *úd From Middle English utmost, utemest [and other forms], from Old English ūtmest, ūtemest [and other forms], from ūt, ūte (“out;

definition: Being unoccupied.
example: Sky was set above earth, land ringed with sea, / Chaos retired to its own vacancy ….
etymology: From Late Latin vacantia. Doublet of vacance.

definition: The percentage of all rental units (as in hotels) that are unoccupied or not rented at a given time.
A lot on which there are no permanent buildings.
A dwelling (a second home) where you live while you are on vacation.
An area where many people go for recreation, holidays or other purposes.
Taking a vaccine as a precaution against contracting a disease.
etymology: From vaccinia, a cowpox infection. Ultimately from Latin vacca (“cow”). Coined by Edward Jenner (1749-1823) in 1798. Jenner infected people with weakened cowpox viruses (vaccinia), to immunise them against smallpox.

definition: An electrical home appliance that cleans by suction.
A gauge for indicating negative atmospheric pressure.
Characteristic of false pride; having an exaggerated sense of self-importance.
example: Vain about her clothes.
etymology: From Middle English veyn, from Old French vain, from Latin vānus (“empty”).

definition: A long depression in the surface of the land that usually contains a river.
etymology: From Middle English vale, from Old French val (“valley”), from Latin vallis, valles. Displaced native Old English dell.

definition: A sweetheart chosen to receive a greeting on Saint Valentine's Day.
example: Will you be my valentine?
etymology: From Saint Valentine's Day (“day of celebration of romantic love”).

definition: The act of validating; finding or testing the truth of something.
etymology: From Middle French validation. By surface analysis, validate + -ion.

definition: The quality of being valid and rigorous.
etymology: From valid + -ity, borrowed from Middle French validité, from Late Latin validitas.

definition: An infection of the lungs and skin characterized by excessive sputum and nodules.
An appraisal of the value of something.
example: He set a high valuation on friendship.
etymology: From Middle French valuation, noun of action from valuer, from Old French valoir.

definition: A reserve fund created by a charge against profits in order to provide for changes in the value of a company's assets.
A reserve fund created by a charge against profits in order to provide for changes in the value of a company's assets.
An assessment that reveals more about the values of the person making the assessment than about the reality of what is assessed.
A structure in a hollow organ (like the heart) with a flap to insure one-way flow of fluid through it.
etymology: From Middle English valve, from Latin valva (“double door, valve”). Doublet of valva.

definition: The leading units moving at the head of an army.
etymology: From Middle English vandgard, vaunte garde, vaunt garde, wantgard, from advaunte-garde, avauntgard with aphesis, from Old French avangarde, avant-garde, avantgarde, from avant (“before; in front”) + garde (“guard”).

definition: Long bean-like fruit; seeds are used as flavoring.
A flavoring prepared from vanilla beans macerated in alcohol (or imitating vanilla beans).
example: Vanilla extract makes these cookies taste great, but the straight extract tastes bad because the alcohol hasn't evaporated yet.

definition: Having passed out of existence.
example: Vanished civilizations.

definition: Feelings of excessive pride.
example: It is a vanity to say that if two stones are dropped from a tower, the heavier will experience the greater acceleration.
etymology: From va(i)n + -ity, from Middle English vanite, from Old French vanité, from Latin vānitas, from vānus, whence English vain. Doublet of vanitas.

definition: A vain and frivolous lifestyle especially in large cities.
A visible suspension in the air of particles of some substance.
etymology: From Middle English vapour, from Anglo-Norman vapour, Old French vapor, from Latin vapor (“steam, heat”).

definition: A room that can be filled with steam in which people bathe; ‘vapour bath’ is a British term.

A stoppage in a pipeline caused by gas bubbles (especially a stoppage that develops in hot weather in an internal-combustion engine when fuel in the gas line boils and forms bubbles that block the flow of gasoline to the carburetor).
The pressure exerted by a vapor; often understood to mean saturated vapor pressure (the vapor pressure of a vapor in contact with its liquid form).
A quantity that can assume any of a set of values.
An event that departs from expectations.
example: All breeds of dog are variants of the species “Canis lupus familiaris”.
etymology: From Old French variant, from Latin variāns, the present active participle of variō (“to change”). First attested in c. 1380.

definition: Edible viscera of a butchered animal.
A British abbreviation of ‘university’; usually refers to Oxford University or Cambridge University.
etymology: First attested in the mid-17th century. Clipping of univarsity, reflecting an archaic pronunciation of university.

definition: An award earned by participation in a school sport.
Become different in some particular way, without permanently losing one's or its former characteristics or essence.
example: You should vary your diet. Eating just bread will do you harm in the end.
etymology: From Middle English varien, from Old French varier, from Latin variō (“to change, alter, make different”), from varius (“different, various”); see various.

definition: Of or relating to or having vessels that conduct and circulate fluids.
example: Vascular constriction.
etymology: From New Latin vasculāris, from Latin vasculum, diminutive of vas (“vessel”).

definition: The vessels and tissue that carry or circulate fluids such as blood or lymph or sap through the body of an animal or plant.
An open jar of glass or porcelain used as an ornament or to hold flowers.
example: A vase of flowers.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French vase, from Latin vās. Doublet of vas.

definition: Scandent subshrub of southeastern United States having large red-purple bell-shaped flowers with leathery recurved sepals.
To an exceedingly great extent or degree.
example: He had vastly overestimated his resources.
etymology: From vast + -ly.

definition: A large open vessel for holding or storing liquids.
example: A vat of liquid.

definition: A water-insoluble dye that is applied by reducing the dye to an alkaline form, applying the dye, then regenerating the insoluble dye by oxidation in the material; used for dyeing cotton.
The part of algebra that deals with the theory of vectors and vector spaces.
Nutlike seed of a South American palm; the hard white shell takes a high polish and is used for e.g. buttons.
A small garden where vegetables are grown.
Perennial prostrate mat-forming herb with hoary woolly foliage.
A plant fiber from the kapok tree; used for stuffing and insulation.
Soup made with a variety of vegetables.
example: I made a creamy vegetable soup with carrots, celery, tomatoes, and potatoes.

definition: A waxy substance obtained from plants (especially from the trunks of certain palms).
All the plant life in a particular region or period.

definition: A distinct patch or grouping of plants that can be distinguished from other units.
A garment that covers the head and face.

definition: A blood vessel that carries blood from the capillaries toward the heart.

etymology: From Middle English veine, borrowed from Anglo-Norman veine, from Latin vēna (“a blood-vessel; vein; artery”) of uncertain origin. See vēna for more. Doublet of vena. Displaced native edre, from ǣdre (whence edder).

definition: Smooth and soft to sight or hearing or touch or taste.
etymology: From Middle English velvet, velwet, veluet, from Old Occitan veluet, from Vulgar Latin *villutittus, diminutive of villūtus, from Latin villus (“shaggy hair, tuft of hair”). Cognate with French velours.

definition: A solitary wasp of the family Mutillidae; the body has a coat of brightly colored velvety hair and the females are wingless.
The annual woody vine of Asia having long clusters of purplish flowers and densely hairy pods; cultivated in southern United States for green manure and grazing.
Common grass with slender stems and narrow leaves.
Young leaves widely used as leaf vegetables; seeds used as cereal.
Tall European perennial grass having a velvety stem; naturalized in United States and used for forage.
Any of various plants of the genus Verbascum having large usually woolly leaves and terminal spikes of yellow or white or purplish flowers.
Arborescent perennial shrub having palmately lobed furry leaves and showy red-purple flowers; southwestern United States.
Someone who promotes or exchanges goods or services for money.
The act of taking revenge (harming someone in retaliation for something harmful that they have done) especially in the next life.
example: Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman vengeaunce, from Old French vengeance, venjance, from vengier (“to avenge”). Analysable as venge + -ance.

definition: Toxin secreted by animals; secreted by certain snakes and poisonous insects (e.g., spiders and scorpions).
example: The serious artist […] [is] obsessed by his material; it’s like a venom working in his blood and the art is the antidote.
etymology: From Middle English venym, from Old French venim, from Vulgar Latin *venīmen, from Early Medieval Latin venīnum, from Classical Latin venēnum (“drug; poison;

definition: A hole for the escape of gas or air.
