example: This toxin impairs ventilation by causing inflammation in the bronchioles.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French ventilation, from Old French ventilacion, from Late Latin ventilatio, from Latin ventilo. Morphologically ventilate + -ion.

definition: A mechanical system in a building that provides fresh air.
example: She was continually adjusting the ventilation.

definition: Wealth available for investment in new or speculative enterprises.
Capitalism that invests in innovative enterprises (especially high technology) where the potential profits are large.
A speculator who makes money available for innovative projects (especially in high technology).
etymology: From venture capital + -ist.

definition: The word class that serves as the predicate of a sentence.
example: The word “speak” is an English verb.
etymology: From Middle English verbe, directly from Latin verbum (“word, verb”), reinforced by Old French verbe, from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰo-. Doublet of verve and word.

definition: One of the two main constituents of a sentence; the predicate contains the verb and its complements.
A region marking a boundary.
example: I was on the verge of tears.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French verge (“rod or wand of office”), hence "scope, territory dominated", from Latin virga (“shoot, rod stick”), of unknown origin.

definition: Additional proof that something that was believed (some fact or hypothesis or theory) is correct.
example: The detective needs verification of your whereabouts last night.
etymology: From Middle French verification (modern French vérification) or its etymon Medieval Latin vērificātiō. By surface analysis, verificate + -ion.

definition: Any plant of the genus Veronica.
etymology: Named after Saint Veronica.

definition: Having great diversity or variety.
example: His vast and versatile erudition.
etymology: From Latin versātilis (“turning easily”), from versātus, past participle of versō (“to turn, change”), frequentative of vertō (“to turn”).

definition: A composition written in metrical feet forming rhythmical lines.
A line of metrical text.
A bank so steep that the plane's lateral axis approaches the vertical.
A stabilizer that is part of the vertical tail structure of an airplane.
A labor union that admits all workers in a given industry irrespective of their craft.
A direction in music; to be played very loudly.
A direction in music; to be played very softly.
Provide with power and authority.
example: They vested the council with special rights.
etymology: Derived from French veste (“a vest, jacket”), from Latin vestis (“a garment, gown, robe, vestment, clothing, vesture”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéstis, from *wes- (“to be dressed”) (English wear).

definition: A small pocket in a man's vest.
Of or relating to veterinarians or veterinary medicine.
example: Max used all his veterinary knowledge to save the goose stuck in the fence.
etymology: From Latin veterīnārius, from veterīnus and veterīnae (“cattle;"beasts of burden/of draught"”); compare with veterinarian.

definition: The branch of medicine that deals with the diagnosis and treatment of diseases and injuries of animals (especially domestic animals).
A school teaching veterinary medicine.
A doctor who practices veterinary medicine.
A vote that blocks a decision.
example: An outer detector (OD) region will act as both a passive shield for low energy backgrounds and an active veto for cosmic ray muons.
etymology: From Latin vetō (“to forbid”).

definition: A percussion instrument similar to a xylophone but having metal bars and rotating disks in the resonators that produce a vibrato sound.
Vigorous and animated.
example: A vibrant group that challenged the system.
etymology: From French vibrant, from Latin vibrans, present participle of vibrare (“to vibrate”). See vibrate.

definition: The act of vibrating.
etymology: From French vibration, from Latin vibrātiō (“a shaking or brandishing”), from vibrō (“shake, vibrate”); see vibrate. Morphologically vibrate + -ion.

definition: With the order reversed.
example: She hates him and vice versa.

definition: Relating to a vice president or vice-presidency.
example: Vice-presidential debates.

definition: One trouble leads to another that aggravates the first.
One trouble leads to another that aggravates the first.
Exaggeratedly proper.
Having won.
example: The victorious entry.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin victōriōsus, from victōria (“victory”), from victor (“conqueror”). Displaced native Old English siġefæst.

definition: A celebration following a victory in a battle or sports competition.
The angle included by a photographic lens.
A close observer; someone who looks at something (such as an exhibition of some kind).
example: Television viewers.
etymology: From Middle English vewer; equivalent to view + -er.

definition: A mental position from which things are viewed.
example: We should consider this problem from the viewpoint of the Russians.
etymology: From view + point.

definition: Being one more than seven.
Morally reprehensible.
example: The vile development of slavery appalled them.
etymology: From Middle English vile, vyle, vyl, from Anglo-Norman ville, Old French vil, vile, from Latin vīlis.

definition: A plant with a weak stem that derives support from climbing, twining, or creeping along a surface.
example: They picked the grapes off the vine.

definition: Slender arboreal snake found from southern Arizona to Bolivia.
Sour-tasting liquid produced usually by oxidation of the alcohol in wine or cider and used as a condiment or food preservative.
etymology: From Middle English vynegre, from Old French vinaigre from Old French vyn egre, based on Latin vīnum (“wine”) + Latin ācer (“sour”). Displaced Old English æċed (survived in Middle English eced).

definition: Flies whose larvae feed on pickles and imperfectly sealed preserves.
etymology: So called because it may breed in imperfectly sealed preserves and in pickles.

definition: Deciduous shrubby tree or eastern North America with compound leaves that turn brilliant red in fall and dense panicles of greenish yellow flowers followed by crimson acidic berries.
A farm of grapevines where wine grapes are produced.
example: The vineyard of Château Margaux stands as the producer of one of the world's greatest and most sought-after red wines.
etymology: Equivalent to vine + yard;

definition: Any of the numerous plants of the genus Viola.
etymology: From Latin viola (“violet”).

definition: Fail to agree with; be in violation of; as of rules or patterns.

etymology: From Middle English violat, from Classical Latin violātus.

definition: A crime less serious than a felony.
example: Nahh saying that to bro is actually a violation 💀.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French violation, from Latin violātiō (“injury, profanation”), from violō (“to treat with violence; to maltreat; to violate, defile, profane”). Morphologically violate + -ion.

definition: A violent weather condition with winds 64-72 knots (11 on the Beaufort scale) and precipitation and thunder and lightning.
A violently fast stream of water (or other liquid).
In a violent manner.
example: They attacked violently.
etymology: From Middle English violently; equivalent to violent + -ly.

definition: Having a violet color.
Having a violet color.
Of pink tinged with lavender.
Light violet and dark purple.
A bow used in playing the violin.
(music) the family of bowed stringed instruments.
A lesson in playing the violin.
Someone who makes violins.
etymology: From violin + maker.

definition: The section of an orchestra that plays violins.
Pneumonia caused by a virus.
Human conception without fertilization by a man.
example: Many religions and traditions have myths about a virgin birth.
etymology: From virgin + birth.

definition: Forest or woodland having a mature or overly mature ecosystem more or less uninfluenced by human activity.
Wool not used before; wool not processed or woven before.
A reflected optical image (as seen in a plane mirror).

(computer science) memory created by using the hard disk to simulate additional random-access memory; the addressable storage space available to the user of a computer system in which virtual addresses are mapped into real addresses.

A hypothetical three-dimensional visual world created by a computer; user wears special goggles and fiber optic gloves etc., and can enter and move about in this world and interact with objects as if inside it.
etymology: Calque of French réalité virtuelle. virtual + reality

definition: (computer science) memory created by using the hard disk to simulate additional random-access memory; the addressable storage space available to the user of a computer system in which virtual addresses are mapped into real addresses.
In essence or effect but not in fact.
example: The strike virtually paralyzed the city.
etymology: From Middle English vertually; equivalent to virtual + -ly.

definition: The difference in value over a period of time of a country's imports and exports of merchandise.
(physics) electromagnetic radiation that can produce a visual sensation.
A phonetic alphabet invented by Melville Bell in the 19th century.
Impairment of the sense of sight.
A printed or written greeting that is left to indicate that you have visited.
A nurse who is paid to visit the sick in their homes.
A professor visiting another college or university to teach for a limited time.
The visual percept of a region.
example: A vista of pleasure to come.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian vista (“view, sight”), from visto, past participle of vedere (“to see”), from Latin vidēre (“to see”). Compare vision, video, visa.

definition: Outward or visible aspect of a person or thing.
One of the cells of the retina that is sensitive to light.
Communication that relies on vision.
The cortical area that receives information from the lateral geniculate body of the thalamus.
Impairment of the sense of sight.
A mental image that is similar to a visual perception.
Impairment of the sense of sight.
A joke whose effect is achieved by visual means rather than by speech (as in a movie).
A red photopigment in the retinal rods of vertebrates; dissociates into retinene by light.
A signal that involves visual communication.
With respect to vision.
example: Visually distorted.
etymology: From visual + -ly.

definition: Having greatly reduced vision.
The maximum amount of air that can be exhaled after a maximum inhalation (usually tested with a spirometer); used to determine the condition of lung tissue.
(biology) a hypothetical force (not physical or chemical) once thought by Henri Bergson to cause the evolution and development of organisms.
Sign of life; usually an indicator of a person's general physical condition.
example: He was still alive but his vital signs were weak.

definition: Data relating to births and deaths and health and diseases and marriages.
example: The Office of National Statistics maintains Britain's vital statistics.

definition: A pill containing one or more vitamins; taken as a dietary supplement.
Evoking lifelike images within the mind.
example: A vivid description.
etymology: The noun sense (a type of marker pen) was genericized from Bic's Vivid Marker brand.

definition: Either of two pairs of folds of mucous membrane projecting into the larynx.
Music intended to be performed by one or more singers, usually with instrumental accompaniment.
Of or relating to a vocation or occupation; especially providing or undergoing training in special skills.
example: Vocational school.
etymology: From vocation + -al.

definition: Training for a specific vocation in industry or agriculture or trade.
A program of vocational education.
A secondary school teaching the skilled trades.
Training for a specific vocation in industry or agriculture or trade.
The popular taste at a given time.
example: Leather is the latest vogue.
etymology: First attested in 1565. Borrowed from Middle French vogue (“wave, course of success”), from Old French vogue, from voguer (“to row, sway, set sail”), from Old Saxon wogōn (“to sway, rock”), var.

definition: Produced with vibration of the vocal cords.
example: Voiced consonants such as ‘b’ and ‘g’ and ‘z’.

definition: A speech sound accompanied by sound from the vocal cords.
Evaporating readily at normal temperatures and pressures.
example: Volatile oils.
etymology: From Middle French volatile, from Latin volātilis (“flying; swift; temporary; volatile”), from volō (“to fly”).

definition: An oil having the odor or flavor of the plant from which it comes; used in perfume and flavorings.
Computer storage that is erased when the power is turned off.
Relating to or produced by or consisting of volcanoes.

Extrusive igneous rock solidified near or on the surface of the Earth.
Out of your own free will.
example: He voluntarily submitted to the fingerprinting.
etymology: From voluntary + -ly.

definition: Tell voluntarily.
example: He volunteered the information.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French voluntaire, from Latin voluntārius (“willing, voluntary”); or from voluntary + -eer.

definition: The matter ejected in vomiting.
etymology: From Middle English vomiten, from Latin vomitāre (“vomit repeatedly”), frequentative form of vomō (“be sick, vomit”), from Proto-Indo-European *wemh₁- (“to spew, vomit”).

definition: Eject the contents of the stomach through the mouth.
example: After drinking too much, the students vomited.

The total number of voters who participated.
One of several districts into which a city or town is divided for voting; each contains one polling place.

etymology: Inherited from Middle English vowe, voue, that from Old French vut, in turn from Latin vōtum (“a promise, dedication, vow”), from vovēre (“to promise, vow”). Not related to avow. Doublet of vote.

definition: Susceptible to attack.
example: A vulnerable bridge.
etymology: From Late Latin vulnerābilis (“injurious, wounding”), from Latin vulnerō (“to wound”).

definition: The wage demanded from management for workers by their union representatives.
An agreement to raise wages.
Floor below which wages are not allowed to fall.
The amount a salary is increased.
example: He got a wage hike.

definition: A schedule of wages paid for different jobs.
A schedule of wages paid for different jobs.
A metal hoop forming the tread of a wheel.
A passenger car that has berths for sleeping.
etymology: From French wagon-lit.

definition: Spare anchor for use in emergency.
A person whose occupation is to serve at table (as in a restaurant).
etymology: From late 14th century Middle English waiter, wayter (“attendant, watchman”). By surface analysis, wait + -er.

definition: A woman waiter.
example: A waitress in a cocktail bar.
etymology: From waiter + -ess.

definition: A formal written statement of relinquishment.
example: I had to sign a waiver when I went skydiving, agreeing not to sue even if something went wrong.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman weyver, from waiver. Date: 1628. By surface analysis, waive + -er.

definition: Any liliaceous plant of the genus Trillium having a whorl of three leaves at the top of the stem with a single three-petaled flower.
A union representative who visits workers at their jobs to see whether agreements are observed.
Ferns having lanceolate fronds that root at the tip.
A light comfortable shoe designed for vigorous walking.
A clock mounted on a wall.
Decoration that is hung (as a tapestry) on a wall or over a window.
example: The cold castle walls were covered with hangings.

definition: Yellow-flowered European plant that grows on old walls and in waste places; an adventive weed in North America.
etymology: From wall + rocket.

definition: Small delicate spleenwort found on a steep slope (as a wall or cliff) of Eurasia and North America.
Receptacle providing a place in a wiring system where current can be taken to run electrical devices.
A decorative paper for the walls of rooms.
example: He is letting her select the wallpapers for the whole house.
etymology: From wall + paper.

definition: Nut of any of various walnut trees having a wrinkled two-lobed seed with a hard shell.

definition: Trees having usually edible nuts: butternuts, walnuts, hickories, pecans.
Oil from walnuts.
Any of various trees of the genus Juglans.
Move about aimlessly or without any destination, often in search of food or employment.
example: The wandering Jew.
etymology: From Middle English wandren, from Old English wandrian (“to wander, roam, fly around, hover; change;

definition: A mixed nerve that supplies the pharynx and larynx and lungs and heart and esophagus and stomach and most of the abdominal viscera.
A public announcement by a law enforcement agency that they desire to question or arrest some person.
etymology: wanted + poster
